utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Today is Monday, 19th of May, 2008. Let me greet the Prosecution, including Mr. Stringer, who is back with us after having left us for quite some time; and good afternoon also to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Khan, it's a pleasure for me to see him again here because we had missed him these past few weeks; let me also greet the accused and everyone assisting us in and around this courtroom. I'm first going to give the floor to the registrar, he has to give us some IC numbers following a number of filings for submission of exhibits by the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted list of documents to be tendered through Witness Damir Zoric. The list submitted by 1D shall be given exhibit number IC 00791. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given exhibit number IC 00792. The list submitted by 3D shall be given exhibit number IC 00793. And the list submitted by 4D shall be given exhibit number IC 00974. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that Mr. Scott wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, each of Your Honours, counsel, all those in and around the courtroom who are assisting us. Your Honour, I need to raise with the Chamber, and I hope we can take it rather briefly because I'm hoping that there won't be -- in light of the circumstances there won't be any objection to this, in fact. In the past several days the Prosecution has received - and again I thank the Defence for providing it - but has received a large volume of material that's either just been translated or not translated yet at all. Since approximately Friday of last week we've received this much material, and, Your Honour, again I'm not saying anything more than that's what we've received. I'm not saying anything about good or bad faith. I do appreciate counsel providing it to us. But the bottom line, Your Honour, is that the Prosecution is once again in a position where we cannot possibly prepare to cross-examination this witness this week. There's just simply too much material that we've received for the first time and we will ask -- we do ask the Chamber to postpone cross-examination to a future date so that we can study this material and obtain it in translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard for the record, Mr. President. On Thursday we provided the Prosecution with a report that was prepared by Mr. Rebic a couple of years ago, and it was only until Thursday that I saw it in translation, that's the report entitled: "My Report at the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees." So they received it the same time that I received it to work from it, number one. Number two -- and that's 1D 02921. Everyone has been provided with it. Number two, if you will see, in the very last line of paragraph 1 it says that this report was done -- the last sentence says was done from his diary, which consists of around 200 pages. When I saw that I asked that Mr. Rebic bring his diary over here in the event the Prosecution wanted it, unlike other UN agencies, for instance, which have appeared before here and have refused to provide their written notes, we are willing to provide all of this to the Prosecution and to everyone else. Those notes -- and I believe that's 1D 02922. Those notes we are not tendering in as evidence. They were provided merely in the event the Prosecution wanted to check what's in the notes to see whether the notes are consistent with this particular report that Mr. Rebic did a couple of years ago. So it was out of courtesy. I could have easily have deleted this line and not requested the notes and nobody would have been the wiser of it. And I am saying that because at times it appears in this courtroom that our integrity is being questioned and I won't say by whom. I'm not suggesting that it's Mr. Scott, but it is a touchy issue with us. So in any event, we -- I have not looked at these 200 pages of notes because they're in Croatian; I cannot read them. Now, I understand the Prosecution's dilemma. I would say that it would be highly inconvenient for Mr. Rebic to come here and the Prosecution was provided with this document. Next I would say that I find it rather alarming that it's -- this is raised now, on Monday, when for instance had I been contacted on Saturday - and I'm making this comment henceforward so everybody can say - and I don't want to set a precedent for the other Defence, but I have absolutely no problem with the Prosecution meeting with our witnesses in The Hague. So they could have met with him, they could have asked to meet with them to go over any portions of the diary. They do have Croatian speakers on their staff, if they wanted to check anything in particular. So I would object to this request of the Prosecution. If, however, the Trial Chamber is inclined to take them up on it, I would say that Dr. Rebic would be scheduled to come back sometime in the fall because, simply, we cannot accommodate the Prosecution in the very near future because our witnesses are more or less locked in. If you look at their positions, it's very difficult to get somebody to commit a whole week of their lifetime without quite a bit of advance notice. So in any event I bring that up and I understand the Prosecution's position, but I want to make sure that they understand that I'm at the same disadvantage as they are, although I do respect their request to have ample time to go through the notes. And again because there are handwritten notes in addition to I guess some typewritten pages, if they wish to consult with Dr. Rebic I have absolutely no problem with that. So the offer is there and my objection is on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me sum up. In these binders here we have exhibits 1D 2921, it's been translated into English and it's entitled: "My Work at the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons." This document was prepared by Mr. Rebic. In the English version this document has 36 pages to be precise. If you are familiar with this case, it should not be tremendous amount of work to read these 36 pages. Furthermore, I believe that during the examination-in-chief the Defence through Mr. Karnavas will raise a number of issues developed in that report. Furthermore, we have a second document, it's a much longer document, it's Exhibit 1D 02922. These are notes, personal notes, written in B/C/S, they have not been translated, and it's a total of 213 pages. These are notes that have been handed over to the Defence counsel, who can't speak B/C/S, during the proofing of the witness. Mr. Karnavas who, since I've known him for two years now, has always demanded that witnesses hand over their personal notes; that's why he's now -- he has submitted these personal notes for the Prosecution to be aware of them. But Mr. Karnavas has added that he would not tender document 2922. That's the way things stand at the moment. The Chamber will consider the request of the Prosecution to decide whether the Prosecution will conduct the cross-examination or not. But without further ado, we'll have the witness brought in. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do want to before the Chamber deliberates on the point, first off I have been very careful. Everyone in the courtroom, of course, is sensitive to their good name, reputation, and good faith, and the Prosecution is no different in that respect than everyone else. And I was once again very careful not to base any of this on any allegation of bad faith. But be that as it may, it doesn't change the bottom line in that the Prosecution has been provided information that it cannot -- it cannot reasonably deal with in the short amount of time that it has now to prepare. I emphasize this, Your Honour, in light of other issues that we've previously brought to the Chamber's attention, and I will briefly remind the Chamber not to consider this issue in isolation. We have a situation where we have been receiving, and Mr. Karnavas knows that he and I have been engaged in ongoing dialogue about this, what the Prosecution continues to consider insufficient Rule 65 ter summaries. They're general. Again, I understand the difficulties of getting with these witnesses and getting the information, but again the bottom line is Rule 65 ter (g) requires meaningful summaries of the facts that the witness is going to put forward to be summarized and provided to both the Chamber, not just the Prosecution but to the Chamber. It is not simply a listing of topics, of positions that the witness has held, or the topics that will be explained. It is the evidence of the witness. It is a summary of the evidence of the facts of the witness that will be put forward. Both the Chamber is at a continuing disadvantage and the Prosecution is at a continuing disadvantage when we do not have adequate summaries. Now, compound that with the fact that for most of these witnesses, many of these witnesses, we also do not have any prior statement of the witness, unlike the Prosecution witnesses in which statements of these witnesses -- of our witnesses were provided sometimes years, literally years in advance, unlike here. So now we have a situation where we're getting in our view, respectful submission, inadequate summaries, no statements, and then trying to prepare and then we get this much material on short notice. And again, I appreciate Mr. Karnavas sending it to us in various pieces over the last couple of days, I appreciate that, but the bottom line, Your Honour, is it does not provide the Prosecution an adequate opportunity to review this material. It is not -- it is simply the rules -- the rules are the rules, and I made the point the other day that if there are rules that apply to everyone, that applied to the parties and apply to the Chamber. The rules require a certain process to be followed in terms of disclosure, and this is not -- this is not the process. It is not up to the Prosecution to scramble, to put the burden on us to scramble when parties don't meet the rules. And so that is the bottom line. We cannot do this, Your Honour, it's not fair. Whenever this happened in the Prosecution case, what the Chamber consistently did was defer the cross-examination until all the material could be studied, translated and studied, and the Chamber did that consistently during the Prosecution case, and I'm sure the Chamber will not treat the Prosecution different than it treated the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just briefly respond because I do wish to get on with the testimony. When it comes to personal notes, the Prosecution obviously could not compel certain witnesses, albeit they came in from certain organizations where you would expect there to be some sort of transparency, he could not compel them to turn over their notes very well. Here there is no rule that I have to turn over handwritten notes to anyone, and I could have easily not done so and we wouldn't be in this discussion. However, in fairness because the gentleman indicated that this report was made from his handwritten note or his diary I thought, you know, it would be best to turn it over. I received -- when I received this diary was on Thursday, this Thursday, when I received it in English. Without even reading it, I basically glanced at it, my first reaction was: Turn it over. There's no prejudice to the Prosecution in my opinion. Have they read this, they would see, for instance, if they wanted any particular incident they could then go to the note, they have B/C/S speakers. So it's not at their disadvantage, that's number one. Number two, I know that there's an ongoing dialogue and to the extent the Prosecution wishes additional information, we do provide it. For instance, there was one witness, I won't mention his name because he's a protected witness, but they asked for additional information. I brought it to their attention that, number one, the OTP took a statement from that particular witness in 1996. That statement in and of itself covers the entire testimony. OTP statement taken from a witness over a period of two days in 1996. That witness also testified and Mr. Scott was the one that cross-examined the witness. So how can that -- what more do they need? He's going to be speaking about the events. The events are locked into a particular set of time, time frame. With this particular witness let's be realistic also. Mr. Zoric testified, Mr. Zoric was the number two. If you look at the documents that we intend to go through with Mr. Rebic, many, many, many of them have already gone through -- we've gone through Dr. Zoric. The subject matter is the same. So there's -- there are no real surprises. Now, I understand as a matter of principle, the Prosecution is laying down their marker for future purposes. I leave it to the Court's discretion, but at some point enough is enough. We have to decide. We're not -- you -- and I just want to say this and I say it with the utmost respect, I know I have my disagreements with some members of the Trial Chamber, but I'll be very, very blunt: This Trial Chamber cannot compel me to provide a statement from a witness. It cannot do so. It's not called for in the Statute, it's not for in the rules, and it would be ultra vires for this Trial Chamber to do so against Dr. Prlic or anyone else in this courtroom at the exclusion of everybody else who has come before this Tribunal. It's an adversarial system. I chose not to go into the mechanics, but Mr. Khan did so in a very eloquent way, but basically this is the way it is. And so I do provide whatever I'm required to provide. If they need additional information, I do. I do so in a timely fashion to the extent that is possible. Now, had I received this document earlier, I would have turned it over earlier, but I understand -- and again, it's not -- this is not directed towards Mr. Scott, but there seems to be an impression that's being created that somehow we are being less than forthright with the parties and the Court. And I want to make sure that at least to the extent that I am aware of the Prlic Defence, every single member of the Prlic Defence is extremely professional, ethical, and honest and if there is an error I take full responsibility. But in this instance, when I get it I turn it over. And like I said, I saw the 200 pages and my first reaction was my God, now I've got to turn it over. And my second reaction was to my colleague is the Prosecution is more likely than not going to ask for a continuance of the cross-examination because I know what their position is going to be. So I leave it to -- I leave it to Your Honours. But I would say before you hear -- before you make a decision perhaps we should hear the direct examination, and then I would also urge that we go forward, at least with some cross, so that the gentleman doesn't have to come back. He's very old. He's had heart surgery. He has an extremely busy schedule. It's very difficult for me to meet with him, and I don't think it's convenient for me to be telling every one of my witnesses you're going to have to come back because this is a good way for me to lose witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate on this. We've just spent 20 minutes dealing with this, and I have two things to say. First of all - and this is my own personal opinion - as the Presiding Judge I have to say this. We have a document here that's 216 pages long. It's a document in B/C/S. Of course that can be problematic, but when I turn my eyes to the Prosecution desks I see here that we have four representatives of the OTP and one is enough, the others could very well meet with a staff member of the OTP who can speak B/C/S and during the examination-in-chief they could work on these 216 pages to find out if there's anything of importance in these 216 pages. Secondly, this problem is likely to occur time and time again. I've had a look at Mr. Prlic's witness list until the 3rd of July. I've noted that a number of prominent persons will come and testify. They probably have personal notes, and we run the risk of being faced with this situation time and time again. If a witness arrives and submits his personal notes to Mr. Karnavas, 200, 400, 1.000 pages of notes, then the Prosecution will tell us, We can't cross-examine. This situation may occur time and time again because the witnesses we are going to have in the near future are not victims; they are people who held high positions. And if these witnesses come here with their personal notes, we might be faced with documents in B/C/S counting hundreds of pages. We can't in every case postpone the cross-examination. These are inherent constraints we have here. We have to take this into account. Let me remind you that the burden of proof rests on the Prosecution, and based on this principle the Defence is not obligated to anything. The only thing the Defence has to do is when calling its own witnesses to provide a list of the exhibits and to provide summaries. These are the obligations of the Defence based on the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. What concerns me is about the following witnesses - I'm not going to give their names, some of them may be protected - but I'm concerned that we might find ourselves in the same situation time and time again. Let me add that anybody who is familiar with this case is in a position and has to be able to deal with any document. What do the Judges do when they arrive at the hearing? Well, they receive three binders and they have to be ready to work with these binders; otherwise, they could say, Oh, we have to stop for two weeks and we'll postpone the hearing for two weeks. But why not? But then the trial would go on for about 20 years. Each and every one of us has to make an effort here. Of course some requests are legitimate, but there comes a time when we shouldn't go too far. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest respect I must say that I'm shocked by the Chamber's -- by the President's comments just now. What I've just heard the Chamber say is: We don't have time to enforce the rules and if the rules can't be complied with so be it. I will not be put on the defensive on this issue, I will not have the Prosecution put on the defensive this issue. There are rules to be enforced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will stop and then I will continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there must be a mistake in the translation. I've never said that -- you always interrupt me when I speak, but before you do so check what I've said. I've never said what you've just told us about the Rules. I've said that as part of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence the only obligation of the Defence is to provide the list of the exhibits and the summaries. That's what I said. I didn't say anything more. You are interpreting my words. Of course there might be a mistake in the translation, and that's why you may have not quite understood what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, again with great respect what I was referring to was your comments just a few meant moments ago when you were concerned that this same procedure, this same situation, can develop in the future and that if it happened it would result in delaying the trial. That is my concern. And what the Chamber has -- excuse me, not the Chamber, Mr. President, what you were then saying is that because it would delay the trial we can't follow the Rules and that is fundamentally inconsistent as I was beginning to say when I deferred back to the President. Your Honour, I will not be put in the defensive -- on the defensive on this issue. I will not have the Prosecution put on the defensive on this issue. The Prosecution is doing its job. There are rules to be followed here. I did not accuse Mr. Karnavas of any bad faith, but the bottom line is the rules have to be enforced and there are disclosure rules and they have not been followed, perhaps in good faith, they have not be satisfied in this case. I will not be the one in this courtroom to be put on the defensive when I am the one that's only just now received this material, and it is not up to my staff to stand up all night trying to read 213 pages of untranslated B/C/S material just so this trial can go forward when people don't comply with the rules. And I am shocked. I am shocked by the President's statements. I hope the rest of the Chamber will have a more reasoned view and that the Chamber will do what it's done in the past and there will be an opportunity for the Prosecution to have this material in ample time translated to be able to prepare for cross-examination which is its right to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, I can't let Mr. Scott say that. Mr. Scott is shocked. He's very easily shocked. I don't know why. He's shocked hearing me say that when I look at the table of witnesses who will come and testify until the 3rd of July I find that there are a lot of witnesses who may, who may, bring personal notes when they come to The Hague. And then in that particular situation at the weekend Mr. Karnavas will submit these notes to the Prosecution because the gentleman will come on the 9th of June, for example, is likely to produce personal notes. He may do so, he might not do so. But if he does so, if he submits personal notes we will find ourselves in the exact same situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I don't understand why you're shocked --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when I'm talking about something that could very well happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- sorry, I do apologies. Your Honour I do apologies. This is not a jack-in-the-box system of justice in which people can simply stand up and start responding to the Bench as if there is an equality between all three parties in the court --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- specifically his comments to me, and I asked to respond directly to the President's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if I can just say something that may assist and of course my learned friend can respond with your leave at the end. And Your Honour, it is with an endeavour to assist. One cannot but help recollect the comments of your learned brother, Judge Prandler, some weeks ago in which he drew attention to the vast amount of time that has been taken to procedural matters. Your Honour, in making submissions, it behooves us not as laypersons but as attorneys who are licensed to practice and who should have and who have experience as lawyers to follow a somewhat disciplined approach. Now, Your Honour, just looking at this instance in the court for the last half an hour, it views -- it displays, in my respectful submission, a microcosm of one of the maladies that have afflicted, in my very respectful submission, some of the proceedings. My learned friend started off with a specific application, he said it would not take long, and it referred in essence to the documents produced by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas and in particular, perhaps, 1D 02922, and that was the thrust of the application. That was responded to by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas. Now, the first point I have to make is that under the Rules there is no right of reply to an issue. All pertinent grounds must be raised in an application of first instance. My learned friend stood up and in his reply he expanded his objection to these old chestnuts, if I put it colloquially, about the insufficiency of a 65 ter statement, his being -- his lament at not having prior statements. Your Honours, how many times in a court of law does it behoove the parties to go over the same ground? It expands the ambit of procedural matters completely unnecessarily. My learned friend has said and his exact words were "rules are the rules." He's very adamant the rules are the rules, that I agree. Well, in that case my learned friend is a lawyer and I do -- I do have to say with the greatest respect, one should refer to the rules and say in what respect is there non-compliance. Of course the duties of the Prosecution under 66 and 68 are specific, they are different to the obligations of the Defence because they emanate from the burden of proof and their responsibility to bring a case and to prove it. Your Honour, in this instance of course we don't have, to use that awful phrase, and we don't have a dog in this fight, but in relation to 1D 02922 there's no obligation on the Defence to produce documents that they're not seeking to use. If my learned friend has produced a document over and beyond the call of the Rules simply to let my learned friend have a view of the case, but is not seeking to use that document, I don't see for the life of me how a party that has no right to such document can be said to be prejudiced. But, Your Honour, be that as it may, I think it only behooves us to be rather disciplined as lawyers in our approach to all matters, legal submissions and responses, but unless we, you know, grasp this nettle these are going to be very painful proceedings and much longer than they should otherwise be. Your Honour, I do apologise to my learned friend for interrupting him. It is with a spirit of cooperation. Of course he can respond to whatever I have said that may have merit or not have merit and of course to what Mr. President said earlier with their leave. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Scott, for the umpteenth time you have the floor to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's really not necessarily either, with all respect. I am quite confident that if the -- that if anyone who cares to take the time to analyse the amount of time spent on procedural matters in this case, I am a hundred per cent confident that the Chamber would find the Prosecution has spent a hugely small, incontestably small percentage of that time. I will not apologise. I will not apologise for raising issues which I believe that I'm professionally obligated to raise in the interests of the Prosecution, in the interests of the victims and the international community which we represent. I will not apologise for that if I think that I'm doing my job, and again I think we have used our time, the record will show, quite sparingly. Now, I did not expand our position except to answer the questions that Mr. Karnavas has raised and then, Your Honour, points that you made. I was speaking in direct response to that. We believe that these are important matters, Your Honour, and it's because I agree with you that this could arise with future witnesses that it can be dealt with. If that's the case then Mr. Karnavas knows who his witnesses are, and these materials can be obtained in advance in a timely way and submitted for translation. Now, why -- you know, he knows which witnesses are coming between now and July, there is a telephone, he can call them up, have you made prior statements, are there additional documents that you provided to us, did you keep a diary, and if so it can be provided. But, you know, it's not my fault. Maybe it's not Mr. Karnavas's completely fault, but it's certainly not the Prosecution's fault that we only received this material just now and the remedy is not to ignore it. The remedy is not to dismiss the Prosecution's concerns. The remedy is indeed to enforce the rules about disclosure and fair conduct. Fair conduct. I'm a little bit -- I'm a little bit, I have to say I'm a little bit - what should the word should I use? - perturbed, concerned when I say, Well, the Rules don't require. Well, I'm sure that everyone in the courtroom -- well, presumably everyone in the courtroom wants to conduct themselves in a fair way and not do the bare minimum, the bare minimum that may perhaps the Rules require. And that's the position, Your Honour. So let me be very clear with the greatest respect to the Chamber, and I have great respect for all four of you. But in all fairness I am not apologetic for our position. I will not be defensive about it. There are rules about disclosure, we have just received it, and we will insist in the future, and if it happens again, Your Honour is absolutely right, I will be on my feet again. And if it means doing it every time I'll do it every time for the Rules to be enforced in a fair and reasonable way. That's all that the Prosecution has asked for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have the witness brought in. The Trial Chamber recalls that it has granted four hours for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me first check that you can hear me. If you can hear me, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please, sir, state your name, first name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Adalbert Rebic, the 23rd of January, 1937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am under the impression that I can't hear the French booth, but I see that you were born on the 23rd of January, 1937. Can you tell me if you have a current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have retired from the Zagreb university where I used to teach at its faculty of theology. Partially, however, I'm still busy as the director of Krscansk Sadasnjost which is a publishing house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you had an opportunity to testify before a national or international court as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I appear before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some brief explanations on my part. Mr. Karnavas is the counsel you're bound to have met, probably he told you the same thing, but I'd rather say it again. This is a trial of Anglo-Saxon type, if I may say, and you are to answer, first, questions put to you by Mr. Karnavas, who's on your left. He is going to ask questions of you and submit documents to you. You have four Judges in front of you. They too, based on the documents or based on your answers, can ask questions in order to shed light on specific parts of your answers. The Prosecutor is sitting on your right. As part of the cross-examination - it may be this week or later, the Trial Chamber will decide later - the Prosecutor will ask questions as part of the cross-examination. But the counsel representing other accused because Mr. Karnavas is the representative of Mr. Prlic but there are other accused, their counsel can after Mr. Karnavas has completed his examination-in-chief ask questions as part of the cross-examination carried out by other accused. You are a professor, so you know better than anyone that you are supposed to answer briefly, whilst the questions put to you may be very complex and complicated. So do endeavour to highlight the most relevant parts in your answers because everything you are about to say is going to be recorded. This is the reason why you have on the screen before you our words as they have been interpreted. If you do not understand the meaning of a question, do not hesitate to ask the one putting the question to you to reformulate it. As a matter of a rule we have a break every an hour and a half and they last 20 minutes. But if at any time you do not feel, you want to have a break, if you need a rest, there again do not hesitate to say so and I shall call for a break. We're supposed to be sitting in the afternoons until Thursday. On Thursday we will finish at the latest around 6.30 in the afternoon, 6.25 or 6.30. You have just made a solemn declaration; therefore, you are a witness of the Court and you're not supposed to have any contact with Defence counsel or with the Prosecutor, otherwise your testimony would not have the same value. If at any point in time you feel a need to ask a question of the Judges, we're here to answer any question you may have. This being said, I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Karnavas. He has - and I'm looking at the watch - he has four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon again Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission and unless there are objections from the Prosecution I would ask some leading questions regarding the gentleman's background, just the background, to save some time. As I understand it, Dr. Rebic, you hold a doctorate degree in theology or philosophy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You got your Ph.D. in the Gregorian institute or the Gregorian Papal University in Rome; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is correct; however, my Ph.D. is in theology rather than philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In theology, that's correct. And, in fact, you did your dissertation in Germany?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And speaking of languages, you speak several languages, including German, French, English, I believe Hebrew, you understand fluently Slovenian, and there might be another language -- and you speak Italian as well?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is right. I spent eight years studying in Rome; however, I must say that some of my languages are better than others. I used to teach Hebrew, for years I taught at the university. The Hebrew language that the Old Testament and the Bible had been written in. I can understand the Israelites in Israel; however, it is a living language that they use there and I have a certain degree of difficulty understanding it since one needs to be immersed into it to be able to understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand it you've published over 20 books, and you've written over 20 books, and you have also translated over 35; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with respect to your testimony here today and for the rest of the week, from 1991 to 1996 you were the head of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees for the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe for one year, I believe it was 1995, you served as a minister without portfolio?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get into the documents I thought I would ask a series of general questions that might be of some importance to everyone and it will lay out more or less the outline for the remainder of your testimony on direct examination. First and foremost, as I understand it, over the years, 1991 to 1996, you had many opportunities to be with Dr. Tudjman, who was the president of the Republic of Croatia at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You sat at meetings, government meetings, where he presided?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, government meetings and at various meetings at which the issue of displaced persons and refugees was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's the Prosecution's theory that President Tudjman had a vision, a wish, to recreate the Banovina Hrvatska, and in attempting to do so he was trying to carve up Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period that you were serving as the head of the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees. Now, could you please describe to us and tell us based on your insight, based on your association with Dr. Tudjman and your participating -- participation in meetings what you believe Dr. Tudjman's position was concerning the Banovina Hrvatska and the carving up of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tudjman was a historian; as such, he knew very well that Croats and Serbs before World War II had agreed to provide greater autonomy to Croats. In that regard, Croatia had been given a part of the territory of what is today Bosnia-Herzegovina, where they made up the majority of the population. That entity, the Banovina, fell through in 1944 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1941.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when the independent Republic of Croatia was created, the so-called NDH. As a historian who was concerned with the fate of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Tudjman busied himself with an idea of reviving the old agreement between the Serbs and Croats. He didn't break up Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before Tudjman we had the Serbian aggression, the Serbian aggression caused Bosnia-Herzegovina not only to come under attack but also to break up. When the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina decided to become independent, much the same the Croatian and Slovenian citizens had done before them, it was then that Dr. Tudjman, who by that time had become the president of the Republic of Croatia, accepted that fact. Croatia was the first, if I'm not mistaken, to recognise the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which became internationally recognised at some point. He respected its borders and integrity. In different negotiations there were attempts to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina into certain parts within its state borders, and I have in mind the cantons. It was Tudjman who was always trying to make sure that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be not left behind since they lived there for 13 centuries and he wanted to ensure their survival alongside the other two peoples, the Serbians and the Bosniaks. They were supposed to be a constituent part of that state of Bosnia-Herzegovina alongside the other two peoples. It is my belief and my impression he stood by that position until his death. After Bosnia-Herzegovina had been recognised, he never wanted to tamper with its integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees, it has been alleged that it played a part in a joint criminal enterprise in that at some point part of this criminal enterprise was to ethnically cleanse Bosnia-Herzegovina of its Muslim population in certain areas, and your office was used as sort of a transit centre, you used camps as transit centres in order to get Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina as far away from Bosnia-Herzegovina with the expectation or hope that they would not return. Let me ask this question. To your understanding, while you were there as head of the office, was your office used in any way for any criminal purposes?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: No, never. Our office was a humanitarian entity rather than a political one. Our main task was to work under difficult wartime conditions in the area of the former Yugoslavia, trying to take care of all those in plight, including our own Croatian citizens who when certain parts of Croatia were occupied, found themselves in dire straits. They had been expelled from their homes and as early as 1991, towards the end of that year, we had around 400.000 displaced persons. When the conflict or the aggression directed at the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took place, from Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, numerous refugees came who were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina seeking refuge in the Republic of Croatia. As the governmental office in charge of displaced persons and refugees, to the extent possible, we provided decent accommodation for them. One needs to bear in mind that at different times we had over 1 million of refugees and displaced persons, meaning that some of them were Croatian citizens while others were people from Bosnia-Herzegovina and we had to take care of them. Approximately that is 12 to 15 per cent of the population of the Republic of Croatia, and that is only the refugees. When we add our own displaced persons to that figure, it rose up to 20 per cent. It would be the same as if, say, today in Germany you had 20 million displaced persons and refugees. Try and imagine how a powerful economy such as the German one would cope with 20 million of displaced persons and refugees. One also needs to bear in mind that Croatia at the time it was under attack itself almost one-quarter of the country had been occupied by Serbs and paramilitary Serb units. The economy was crippled. However, we did muster courage with enormous support of our own citizens and assistance of international organizations, first and foremost the UNHCR and European Union, and we did manage to provide accommodation for the displaced persons and refugees. In no circumstances could one say that Croatia was trying to ethnically cleanse Bosnia-Herzegovina of anyone. That would be playing a very dirty trick upon the Croatian state and its people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. I'm going to ask you a series of questions, rather short answers, and then I can follow up. Okay. Now, first of all, again general questions. Displaced persons/refugees, to your understanding did your office make a distinction between, you know, as far as treatment - we understand the legal difference, what a displaced person is and what a refugee - but did your office make a distinction with respect to treatment, whether it be accommodation, whether it be food, whether it be education? Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: To the extent possible for us, there was no distinction in terms of the treatment of those two categories. To me personally these people were people in plight who needed help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what about accommodation, because we heard one particular witness come here, Azra Krajsek, who had quite a few complaints, allegations I should say, but let's talk about accommodation. Did your office reserve, say, the better accommodation for displaced Croats and then say refugees of Croatian origins from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then sort of gave the Muslims or Serbs or whoever else whatever was left over? What was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: In principle, the procedure applied the same way to everyone, the displaced persons and the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, one needs to know that Croatia came under attack first, and first we had the displaced persons in Croatia. During 1991 these people were being accommodated in various available types of accommodation at the time. What I have in mind are lower-ranking hotels, private homes, and the homes of anyone who was willing to temporarily accommodate them. Of course at the time no one had any idea as to how long the war would last. We all thought that it would cease shortly, and after that we expected the people to be able to return to their homes. It was only after that that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina took place. An enormous amount of refugees flooded over the border from Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that point we were exhausted. It was barely possible to find any accommodation for such great numbers of people. One also needs to bear in mind that in 1992 we had around 400.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, alongside 250.000 our own Croatian citizens who were displaced. In such circumstances, it became a miracle to find good accommodation. For the refugees we tried to come up with certain locations along the Adriatic coast which had been used for vacation spots for workers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, excuse me, I have a problem with the end of your answer. I'd like you to shed some more light on this. You make a distinction between the Serb aggression and the -- later the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we stay with the Serb aggression first of all. I'd like to know when this Serb aggression, as you qualify it, took place apparently in 1991. At that time was there an influx of refugees or displaced persons towards Croatia from BiH? Or you gave a figure of 400.000 people, line 20, page 27, did those people arrive only when there was a conflict in BiH? To sum it up, I'd like to know the following: Were there refugees from BiH during the aggression by the Serbs, regardless of the conflict later on in BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when talking about the aggression, I mean to say that it was done by the Yugoslav People's Army who was controlled at the time by the Serbs and various Serb paramilitary units who attacked Croatia. The same type of aggression occurred, I believe, in April 1992. It was just that at that time it was directed at Bosnia-Herzegovina. The same type of aggression befell our neighbouring state, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since that aggression or war, whichever way you want to put it, first happened against Croatia, 1991, it was first the Croatian citizens who were supposed to flee the occupied territories of eastern and Western Slavonia, the area of the Banovina, Knin, and parts of Dalmatia. They came to the free territory of Croatia where they were accommodated as displaced persons. In 1992, as of the month of April and May, that aggression occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. One just needs to remember the occupation of Sarajevo and other towns. It was at that point that the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina began arriving in Croatia. Temporally speaking, during 1991 we had some 400.000 displaced persons within the borders of the Republic of Croatia. After that, many Croatian citizens also fled to Austria, Slovenia, and Germany. After January 1992 when a truce was achieved and the tensions calmed down, some people began returning to the previously occupied territories from Slovenia and from the free territory of Croatia, slowly bringing down the number of displaced persons in Croatia. In 1992 when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina took place, from one week to the next we had a sharp increase of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had accommodated our displaced persons, our own citizens, during 1991 and we were doing the same thing when it came to the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, irrespective of their ethnicity, irrespective of whether they were Croats, Serbs, or Bosniaks. There was no difference for us. We accommodated them at such locations that we had at our disposal. We urgently requested the Ministry of Defence to put large barracks at our disposal which had been used by the Yugoslav People's Army. These barracks held good infrastructure and were fit to accommodate a large number of people from Bosnia-Herzegovina. We also accommodated them in various tourist facilities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me interrupt you because I'm sure that the Defence counsel will deal with that. I'm interested in what you've said at line 11. You are saying that in 1992 when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina took place there was a sharp increase of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'd like to know the following because here we are dealing with the heart of the matter. From that period on, did you see Muslims arrive in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims coming from Herzegovina? Was there an influx of Muslims coming in, people who following the fighting led by the Serbs left Bosnia and Herzegovina to come to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were refugees from Mostar, both Croats and Muslims, because both felt equally threatened by the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serb paramilitary units. However, most of these refugees in the first few months of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina came from the eastern parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Central Bosnia, from Sarajevo, and from Eastern Herzegovina. At the time Western Herzegovina had been attacked at the very outset, at the very beginning of the aggression, but managed to fight off the aggressors and maintain -- it fended off the threat. The threat stopped at the River Neretva in Mostar so that parts of the JNA owing to the joint forces of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, and the Muslims were pushed back. One should also know that in Herzegovina the majority population are Croats. If I'm not wrong, 96 per cent of the population of Western Herzegovina are of Croatian ethnicity. There were people from there among the refugees of Bosnia-Herzegovina also, and we accommodated them as well. Let me repeat once more that in all these events in accepting and accommodating refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, we did not draw any distinctions between them. We offered the same accommodation to both, and very often they were accommodated together in the same refugee centres. So it could happen, for example, that in Gasinci there were Catholics together with Muslims, and in Gasinci we had a Catholic chapel and a mosque for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you here. We'll probably deal with this later on through Defence counsel's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas, and of course I don't want to stop the proceedings here, but I only have seen one number here which was mentioned by our witness, and Dr. Rebic said that, and I quote him from line 20: "If I'm not wrong, 96 per cent of the population of Western Herzegovina are of Croatian ethnicity." So of course I'm not so well-versed as far as the geographical terms are concerned about Western Herzegovina, but so far we have seen various approaches and numbers there according to the percentage of Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks, and Serbs. So therefore, I wonder if the 96 per cent relates to a territory which could be a bit closely -- in a more closer way to say which territory you had in mind, Dr. Rebic, about the Western Herzegovina as having 96 per cent of Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will tell you some of the towns in that area Medjugorje, which is well-known as the place of the apparition of the blessed Virgin Mary, and the people there are all Catholics; Capljina, is another town; Tomislavgrad, although some people think Tomislavgrad is in Bosnia, the border is not so firm there; Ljubuski is inhabited by Croats. It's hard to say whether it's 94 per cent or 96 per cent because when the census was taken some Muslims declared themselves as Croats. In Mostar it was already the tradition for there to be Muslims who declared themselves as Croats. I personally saw many documents shown to me by Muslims arriving from Bosnia-Herzegovina. These were their school certificates, for example, where it said Croat by ethnicity. So it would be very heard, looking at it from today's point of view, to divide that population into Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, following up on my colleague's question, I must say that this figure of 96 per cent struck me as well. But you seem to be maintaining what you've said. You say that in Capljina the majority of the population was Croat. You also mention Ljubuski, that's not been recorded properly on the transcript -- oh, yes, it has. So Ljubuski as well. And that's why I have the following question. If there were about 100 per cent of Croats, what's the point of ethnic cleansing? If they make up the majority, what's the point? Are you sure about your figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what ethnic cleansing you are referring to in this case. May I ask that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ethnic cleansing, it's mentioned in the indictment where it is stated that the HVO forced populations to move, drove Muslims out, in order for the majority of the population to be Croat. But could that be possible with areas where the population is 96 per cent Croats in the first place? Do you maintain your figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Karnavas, sorry for this digression, but there were a number of points that we needed to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, you had indicated that the -- that in 1992 the aggression had stopped at the Neretva river, and I just want to make sure that we're clear. It was the HVO along with the Muslim forces that repelled the JNA; that was your understanding, correct, not that the HVO was working with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: No, they were against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Both the Croats and the Muslims were against the JNA. In 1992 there was absolute harmony between the Muslims and the Catholics, I'll call them Catholics now, or rather, the Bosniak Muslims and the Bosnian Croats. At that time there was absolute agreement among them and harmony, and wherever they could they put up a joint resistance against the occupiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to follow up on another question, in 1992 when you were asked about refugees coming in to Croatia from Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it be fair to say that they were coming from the Posavina area?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were coming from the Posavina area also; moreover, large numbers were coming from there. There were large areas of Posavina which were occupied by the JNA which was then under Serb command and hundreds of thousands, both Muslims and Croats, crossed the River Sava and arrived in Croatia. In Croatia we gave them refuge, and that was when this refugee camp of Gasinci was built because we had to accommodate thousands of people at very short notice in a single place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So to make sure that I understand, in 1992 when they're coming - and I take it we're talking about the area of what is known as Slavonski Brod, right around that area, as early as 1992 they were being placed, these refugees, into Gasinci?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just those who came from the Bosnian Posavina area, but also from the central parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, I remember that the first refugees we put up in Gasinci came from Sarajevo. If I'm not wrong, there was seven or eight bus loads. So if you calculate there were 50 people per bus, there were about 400 people who arrived from Sarajevo seeking accommodation in the Republic of Croatia. And these were the first persons to whom we were able to offer that former military training-ground which had infrastructure. So we were able to put them up in housing, in buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at some point we know because we heard testimony that large numbers came to the Republic of Croatia to the point that perhaps you could no longer sustain any more refugees. My question now is: Did the Republic of Croatia to your knowledge ever shut down the border for any more refugees, particularly Muslim refugees; in other words, letting the Croats go but shutting down the borders for the Muslims? Did it ever shut down the borders or direct them, say, to Slovenia, go around, go to Slovenia, go to Hungary, but don't come to the Republic of Croatia because we have too many already?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: No. During the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, in that whole period of time, we never closed the borders to refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and never did we send anyone back to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That would have meant sending them back to their death. As for other countries, under the Geneva Convention we could not and were not allowed to force these refugees to go to neighbouring countries because under that convention Croatia is the first neighbouring country which is obliged to protect these refugees and take care of them. Had we sent them to Slovenia, Slovenia would not have accepted them. I remember on one occasion some refugees wanted to go to Slovenia on their own. They arrived at the border crossing in Bregana, where they protested for two days, but the Slovenian police wouldn't let them in so they had to turn back and we accommodated them in Croatia. One should also bear in mind that throughout this time we were working together with international humanitarian organizations and with the UNHCR. We always consulted the representatives of the UN, that is, of the UNHCR, we consulted them daily. We had good relations with them, we took their advice, and in my view their advice was always the following: You take them in, you keep them here, and we will help you and then later on we will see which countries are willing to receive those refugees you are unable to accommodate. At one point in time in a certain period of time, I think it was in August and September 1992, and later on in 1993 also, large waves of refugees, numerous refugees, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, arrived in Croatia and our government sent an appeal to the neighbouring countries asking for help in accommodating these refugees. We received help from Germany, which took in a large number of these refugees and accommodated them in Germany. I remember that the Netherlands, the country I'm in now, sent trains to Karlovac to take part of the refugees and bring them to the Netherlands to be accommodated. We also received help from Austria, Sweden, Denmark, but less from other countries. Italy accepted hardly any refugees. France accepted hardly any. Spain accepted a negligible number. Belgium hardly any refugees, apart from those who had friends or relatives already working in Belgium so that -- well, we kept records so we have precise lists. Apart from the Republic of Croatia where in 1993 there were 250.000 refugees, there were many refugees in Germany. And I won't go into further details, I won't weary the Chamber, but our office regularly drew up reports on this. On three occasions we carried out a census of the displaced persons and refugees; we were prompted to do this by the UNHCR which provided us financial assistance to do so. The first such census was carried out in April, May, and June 1992 when we listed all the displaced persons and refugees --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just stop you here and I'm going to have to interrupt you occasionally so we can keep your answers a little bit shorter. Of course, we do have some statistics that Hungary as well was very generous in taking in large amounts of refugees.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Whereas as I understand, Slovenia, and we'll get into it, Slovenia hardly took any, and in fact there's one great incident in this area called Pineta where they were forcing you to take out refugees from their own resort which is located in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, as regards Hungary in the first wave of aggression against Croatia, Hungary received a large number of Croats and members of ethnic minorities, including Hungarians. They took in about 30.000 people from the Osijek area. They accommodated them very well, they were very well organized. On two or three occasions I visited them in Germany --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Hungary, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to visit our refugees in Hungary. But as soon as the area around Osijek was free of military activity these people all started to come back. So in late 1992 only 3 or 4.000, those who were from Vukovar and eastern Slavonia remained in Hungary because those areas were still under occupation. As for Slovenia, I have to mention with gratitude that at first when Croats were fleeing from Vukovar and other parts of the Republic of Croatia and even Zagreb, we even had refugees from Zagreb in Slovenia because you have to know that the JNA, which was in Serb hands, was very close to Zagreb, it was only some 40 kilometres away from Zagreb. And every day we heard the detonations. You could hear them very well in Zagreb from the bombing, and then some people from Zagreb fled to Ljubljana, but they soon came back. In January 1992 when military activity outside the occupied areas ceased these people came back and only about 20.000 Croatian refugees remained in Slovenia and we gradually had to take them back to the Republic of Croatia. As regards Pineta --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get there. But I want to just touch on some highlights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, should we take a break now or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you like it. We can continue for another five minutes if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just -- and very briefly, because we're going to get into all of this in great detail. We have documents. We know that in 1993, starting in May, sometime in May, June, July, August, there's tension in parts of central Bosnia and Herzegovina between the Croats and the Muslims. My question is - and keep it very brief - at that point to your knowledge did your Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees or did Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, at that point, did they deny entry to any Muslims coming from that area that was as a result of the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims; and if they did receive Muslims, did they begin to discriminate against them, in other words, put them in lower-category facilities, deny them proper access to food, access to education? To your knowledge, please explain this to the Trial Chamber, was there any difference during that period when obviously there were frictions and conflicts between Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina and both were coming in as refugees into the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: At the time that you mentioned, we continued taking in refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina without discriminating in any way but accepting Muslims in the same way as Croats from Bosnia. And then we started using higher-category hotels on the Makarska Riviera, that is when we started using these hotels because we simply had no other possibilities. As the head of the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees I asked the head of the government of the Republic of Croatia to make it possible for us to use the hotels on the Makarska Riviera, and then we accommodated these displaced persons and refugees who had been expelled from Bosnia-Herzegovina without drawing any distinction between Muslims and Croats, although we were aware of the fact that at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not everywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina but in parts of it, there was a conflict between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with that we can take a break, Your Honour, and then continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor back to Mr. Karnavas, the Trial Chamber has to hand down an oral decision, ruling, as to the issue of documents and cross-examination conducted by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber was seized of the following difficulty as raised by the Prosecution; namely, that the Defence disclosed documents 1D 2921 and 1D 2922 and that the Prosecution said they needed time to cross-examine the witness or before cross-examining the witness and had applied for the cross-examination to take place in the fall. The Trial Chamber heard the submissions in reply by the Prlic Defence and by the Stojic Defence team. The Trial Chamber rules that the cross-examination will take place this week. In the event that the Defence would use document 1D 2921, that is 36 pages long and has been translated into English. However, if the Defence were to address issues based on document 1D 2922, which has not been translated, in that case the cross-examination will take place in the fall. For future purposes the Trial Chamber advises the Defence that they should disclose as early as possible any report or personal notes from a witness so that the Prosecution should be in a position to prepare for cross-examination within reasonable time-limits. So there it is. Mr. Karnavas, you're free to raise issues based on 2921, that first document, without any problems since that document has been provided to the Prosecution in English and it is only 36 pages long, it is a chronology of the events; however, if you are to raise issues connected with document 1D 2922, the cross-examination will take place in the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And then again for the record let me make sure that everyone understands that we have asked for all of our witnesses to provide us with all of their notes and notebooks. So we've tried to be diligent, and again this was only translated at the very last moment. As soon as we got it, we gave it over, and of course we've had problems with translation. But we thank the Court for its understanding and we appreciate the Prosecution's concerns and we will try to work with them as much as possible in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Rebic, as far as education is concerned, the issue of education, we had again a Prosecution witness, this Azra Krajsek, who indicated that with respect to education the Muslim refugees were not exercised their right, their fundamental right, to education at Croatian schools. And if you could address that issue, the issue of education. To your knowledge, what sort of education was being provided to displaced persons, refugees, be they Croat, Muslim, or other, because we do know that there were some Serbs that were refugees or displaced persons. We also know that from Sarajevo a large Jewish community was transported over to Zagreb. So could you please comment on that issue.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: In principle, both the refugees and displaced persons had, according to the Geneva Conventions, had the right to education. For Croatian citizens who were displaced from occupied areas, this was a right that was easier to exercise. As for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, this right was somewhat more difficult to exercise for various reasons. The first would be the fact that these people fled their areas in the middle of the school year and more often than not they hoped that they would soon return and continue education in their own midst. The second reason was that they were accommodated in such refugee centres where there was no systematic education, i.e., there was no school for them. So let me put it this way, in principle everybody had the right to be educated. We had cases, for example, in Gasinci where refugee children attended school in Djakovo and according to some data the number of students completed secondary education in Djakovo either in a technical school or in some other schools in Djakovo. Likewise, in Zagreb it was easier to exercise their right than elsewhere because they could get enrolled if they wanted to do so in Croatian schools. I personally know some Muslims who attended and completed secondary school and higher education in Zagreb. They have remained in Zagreb. I still see them and they are very happy in Croatia. They have always been very diligent. Also in other places, like, for example, Split, Pula, and others where there were schools available if they so wanted, and I emphasize, if they wanted to continue education, they could do so. However, since a number of these refugee centres were located outside the urban areas, schooling was possible, we supported that, we organized that, we would establish extra-territorial schools. Among refugees there were also teachers and professors who got involved in the education process, thus we could establish those extra-territorial schools in the refugee centres all over Croatia. This was part of the purview of our Ministry of Culture and Education and partly it was the purview of the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which could and did help us with that to a certain extent. On our part there was no hindrance posed on the refugee education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I understand that your office was located in Zagreb. Could you tell us while you were the head of the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees, whether you visited the various locations; and if so, could you tell us how often and perhaps where, and I'm particularly interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas. You can ask your question later. I thought you were going to go into the answer provided by the witness which you didn't do. Witness, I was going to say Professor, we've had witnesses here who spoke about various curricula. I'm not interested in university curricula; I'm interested in primary and secondary school education. You get a high number of refugees come into Croatia, you said so and other witnesses did too; we're aware of the problem. However, say pupils from elementary school or adolescents in high school, when they arrived in your country, did you set up special classes or curricula that would take into account their own curricula in their country of origin or - and I don't have any information about that - was there a general curriculum in the former Yugoslavia that was applicable and applied in all of the republics or was the teaching specific to a republic; and if so, was that taken on board and into account in Croatia by your ministry for culture and education in order to give young Muslims the same school support as the one they enjoyed in their country? Were any efforts made in that direction? Was their school curriculum adapted to their own specific needs? And I would venture to go even further. Did you also take into account the possible language differences that may have existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have partly answered your question but I will expand. The task of the Office of Refugees and Displaced Persons was primarily to accommodate these people, feed them. After that, allow them to attend school, to have health, security, psychological, and psychiatric health because many of them needed that. At the time, Croatia was occupied and faced with war. The economy was in the doldrums due to the war, and faced with all that to undertake all these activities that you have listed in your question would have really been a very tall order even for a very developed country and a long-term process. We were faced with major time constraints and we just fought fire and we just salvaged what could be salvaged. As far as the education system in the former Yugoslavia is concerned, there were differences among the republics but these differences were not major so that children from Bosnia and Herzegovina, if they so wished, could continue their education in the Republic of Croatia without any problems or adaptations because the system of education was the same across the board. As far as the language is concerned, there were no problems because the language that is used by the citizens of the Republic of Croatia is the same that is used by the civilians of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the former Yugoslavia the name of that language was Croatian or Serbian or Serbian and Croatian. It has to be emphasized that the language that we now call Croatian, since the language has become independent, has its features which are typical of the Croatian language. In the former Yugoslavia we were forbidden to use some of the words and now we are free to use the original Croatian language. I would also like to say that the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, both Muslims and Croats, speak a language that they understand and it's similar to Croatian. There are some differences primarily in the vocabulary. There are no grammatical differences so that no changes were required to the curriculum in that way. As the general curriculum is concerned, I've already said that it was the same across the board and it could easily be adapted. When it comes to the extra-territorial schools that were organized in refugee centres, we would supply them with textbooks that were funded by the Office for Refugees or the Ministry for Education. It was within the purview of the Ministry of Education, but we mutually helped each other by way of me providing the Ministry of Education with information and data and they would then act accordingly. In a nutshell in principle, education, particularly primary and secondary education, was possible; however, in the given situation in some refugee centres it was not very practical or almost impossible to organize that. We did as best as we could. When we couldn't organize education it was not because of the lack of will to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But rather, because of the lack of funds, the lack of teachers, the lack of school room, and so on and so forth. If that refugee crisis had lasted for any longer time, obviously we would have been able to deal with this in a more systematic way. I would like to point at this moment that in the Republic of Croatia we have a lot of problem with the system of school education, we are trying to organize it, but it takes time to put everything together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this comprehensive answer. One moment. There's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Karnavas. I just wanted to check something. I'm not sure I understood something. Witness, you said that the language that is spoken in Croatia today has some specific features so that it was forbidden back then in the former Yugoslavia. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is not easy to answer. In Croatia we speak Croatian. We have spoken it for a long time and it would take me a long way back if I wanted to explain and tell you about the history of the language. However, in the former Yugoslavia in the Republic of Croatia we had a sort of cultural independence, we had our own education system, both primary and secondary, as well our university and obviously this was in Croatian. At that time the Croatian language for political reasons it was Croatian or Serbian or in Serbian it was called Serbian or Croatian. These two languages are rather close to each other; however, let me be very direct in order to help you understand. Because of the predominance of one language, in this specific case Serbian, there have always been efforts to introduce Serbian variance into the Croatian language which pose problems in Zagreb. In Bosnia-Herzegovina the situation was the same, the population spoke the same language as was spoken in Croatia, but the Serbs managed to push their Serb variance a bit more in Bosnia and Herzegovina and mostly this refers to the vocabulary and the syntax which is a bit different between the Croatian and Serbian. Today that -- we are independent in the Republic of Croatia. We use Croatian freely, just like we did before but we are not oppressed in doing so. Nobody is imposing their own vocabulary or syntactic solutions and the same goes for Serbia. As for Bosnia and Herzegovina, the case is that influence has persisted, the influence of the merger between the two languages and I repeat that these two languages are not so different to pose major problems in the two peoples understanding each other. We understand each other perfectly well, we can love each other in that language, and we can hate each other in that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
