utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. My last question on this issue. In the schools where there were the children of refugees, what was the language that was used? Was it the language that you use today, a language that has been freed of the constraints that were prevalent in the former Yugoslavia, or was the language that was then used in the former Yugoslavia used? Which is the language used in those schools for refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the extra-territorial schools in the refugee centres among the Bosniak refugees, i.e., Muslims, the language that was used was the Bosnian or Bosniak variant of the Croatian language, they were free to use that. They even had religion or religious education and they could freely attend classes of Islamic religion, they could use their own expressions, their own terms, just like us Catholics used to use Latin words, the Muslims still use Arabic words. For example, our humanitarian organization is called Caritas in Bosniak it is called Merhamet. Merhamet is not a Slav word and a Bosniak -- and an ordinary Bosniak will not understand the word "Merhamet" but a bit more educated person will understand that Merhamet is an Arabic word that means mercy just like Caritas in our world means mercy. So they were absolutely free to use them and which were Bosniak language if their teachers or professors were able to use it, and I suppose that most of them were able to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You raised an underlying problem. You spoke further on the issue of education but you also addressed the religious issue. These young Muslims, young people of the Muslim faith, the Zagreb government, did they do everything that was necessary for them to have just as a young Catholic Croat who could have religious lessons, for them to have imams who would come and help them continue with their religious education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, absolutely, freely. Among the refugees they had imams that they employed. In Croatia there is an Islamic community with which the Catholic church maintains very good relations. I personally have very good relations with Mr. Sevko Omerbasic, the head of the Islamic community in the Republic of Croatia. And together with him I visited some refugee centres which accommodated Muslims. I visited Varazdin 1 and 2 with him as well as the refugee centre in Pula. They had an absolute freedom to worship their religion. Every refugee centre had a mosque, there was one in Gasinci, there was one on the island of Obonjan, and everywhere else where there was a larger group of Muslims accommodated. We were glad that they were able to do that and they were doing that because the more a person believes in God the better person he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. And just to touch-up on this because I failed to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, you are an ordained priest as well?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am an ordained priest of the Catholic church. I was ordained in 1964, a long time ago, in Rome during the second Vatican council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, as I understand it, aside from presiding in mass and -- at the Cathedral in Zagreb, you've also filled in for priests both in Germany and in France at times?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: I have indeed. I don't know whether this is necessary, but let me say that as a professor in the former Yugoslavia every summer I would spend my summer holidays partly in France with the Carmelite Nuns in St-Germain Anglais Paris, and the other part of the summer I would spend in the Perha [phoen] parish south of Munich where I replaced the local priest. I would usually spend a month there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, and just again because the issue of religion came up in from what I understand it would appear that you are a man that believes in religious tolerance, is it not a fact that you also teach comparative religion and you have studied the various religions, not just Christianity but also Islam, Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Correct. I have taught at the school of theology Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic languages, and my main subject was the interpretation of biblical texts of the old testament, their analysis and synthesis, the biblical theology of the old testament. As for the electives, I would offer my students the Judaism, the teachings, rights, and customs, the rabbi literature from the first to the fourth century A.D. and the relationship between Jewish people and Christians throughout history. I have also published a book on that so that the others can also read about their relationship between Christians and Jewish people. Sometimes they were good, sometimes they were bad, but this should be known so that the evil may be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I've just found out that you're a Catholic priest. It's something I didn't quite catch at the beginning of this hearing. When you became the head of the office you had a double function. You -- is that the case, were you both a priest and the head of this office or were you seconded to the office, did you take leave of your religious duties whilst you were the director of the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I continued performing my religious duties in the Zagreb Cathedral because I have been given an apartment from the Zagreb Cathedral, which means that I live in a church apartment and I have to serve in the Cathedral in return for that. I used to do that while I was leading the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons, but every time I had to pay for a stand-in person. All this time I was a priest and I worked in the office with the permission of my superior, Cardinal Franjo Kuharic. Without his permission I could not have become the head of the government's Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons, and I remained with the office until the end with his permission, and when I resigned it was upon the express wish of Cardinal Kuharic who asked me to return to the university and to place my time fully at the disposal of university because he believed and I believed that once the war was over somebody else could have performed those duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1995 when you were a minister without portfolio, were you a priest then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was still priest with the permission of Cardinal Kuharic and the papal minister, who was then in the Republic of Croatia, asked me for this provision and he told me. If your cardinal, your superior, allows you to do so then the Holy See will not oppose it. If your cardinal is opposed to that then you are not supposed to take the duty and this was done in agreement with the cardinal, so I didn't have any problems or difficulties with Rome. And the explanation for that is fact that this service was of humanitarian nature. It was not a political duty. I was not a member of any party. I was outside any party politics and the only thing I followed was my conscience, and I asked my associates to do the same. None of them were asked to be members of any of the political parties. In other words, the office was a humanitarian office, it was not a political office. At the beginning, the government wanted the church to deal with issues of refugees and displaced persons because it was too much of a burden for the state; however, the church answered the state that it couldn't take the responsibility over because it lacked either resources or money and at the end of the day it was the responsibility of the state and that's how the state finally organized this Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, it was then that you were asked to organize this office?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It was in November, towards the end of that month, when I was asked to organize, together with Mr. Damir Zoric and some others, the office itself. We started from scratch. There was no legislation in place before that and we certainly had no experience. We learned as we went and we have to thank Mr. Comkulato, who was the first UNHCR representative in Zagreb with whom we cooperated extensively. The UNHCR office spent a few months on the same premises as our office did and we closely cooperated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thought that you would insist on having a full answer of your previous question. Witness, you were asked whether you had taught comparative religion including Islam and Buddhism, and you did not answer this question. You only spoke of comparative Christian and Jewish religion. Could you give a more precise answer, please, to the precise question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not teach the history of religion; that was taught by a colleague of mine. It was a different subject, but since we're on that question, if I may, I wanted to say that I am the chief editor of the general religious lexicon which was published in Zagreb in 2002. It contains about 1200 pages rich in illustration and that general religious lexicon is something I worked on with my team for about five or six years. It treats all religions from the prehistoric times, then it covers the central American religions, Asian religions, and the most important religions today of the world, Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Buddhism, as well as all other types of Christianity. In my modest opinion, and according to the views of many other people, it is one of the best lexicons we have in Croatia today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now you mentioned that you were -- you had the assistance of the internationals, you mentioned a Mr. Comkulato, I believe. If you could just briefly tell us during the period while you were the heard of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, to what extent did you come into contact with these so-called internationals, be they from the European Union -- I guess it was the European Community back then, United Nations, NGOs. Would you please explain to us your contact and involvement with them.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Before I answer I just wanted to say that the gentleman's name is Comkulato beginning with a C just for the record. Your question is in place. There were many humanitarian organizations that came to Croatia to offer their assistance in accommodating the displaced persons and refugees. I had daily contact with them. I received them and directed them to various locations where their assistance was needed. Some of them organized shipments of food from abroad, others, for example, the Doctors Without Frontiers, put in place health care in various refugee centres, there were also psychiatrists, there were also people from the Arabic world and their NGOs such as Al Haramija [phoen] and Ikasa [phoen] as well as the Merhamet. From other countries we had good cooperation there as well; however, I would send those to those centres where most of the population were Muslim so that they could assist them as far as possible. In humanitarian terms we were helped the most by the UNHCR. I mentioned that already, as well as the European Union. There were many people coming from the European countries with assistance, in particular Croats for the most part working in Germany, our diaspora in Germany is numerous as well as that in Austria and Switzerland. When the war in Croatia began they were sensitive to our problems. They exhibited great solidarity, and amongst their community in those countries they organized aid for Croatia which arrived daily and I also met with those people daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you here for a second. I had posed a question earlier and you were interrupted and that had to do with visiting the various centres, and I had asked you if you had visited the various centres while you were the head of the office. Of course, we're most interested in Gasinci and Obonjan because there have been some allegations that there was discrimination against the Muslim refugees that were being kept there. So I will ask you to what extent were you visiting centres and did you ever visit those particular two centres?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: I toured all refugee centres as well as the centres where our Croatian citizens were accommodated. Of course I did not do that very frequently. We had system or structure of subordination in place. In the Republic of Croatia we established 21 regional offices all over Croatia more or less corresponding to the borders of the counties in the country. As part of those regional centres, we also had social welfare offices. In each centre I had at least one or two people under my supervision who dealt exclusively with the issue of refugees and displaced persons. I, or rather, they fell under my remit rather than the remit of the minister. I visited some of the centres when there were problems. For example, you can imagine what problems there were if a centre was placed next to a village of 5.000 because the refugee centres were more or less of that size as well. I visited those centres when there were important issues to be resolved in terms of accommodation, food, health care. Both the refugees and displaced persons had their needs and wishes which sometimes could not be met in full and timely by those centres. It is only understandable. On such occasions we would try to come up with a solution. I visited Gasinci on several occasions. I was there once with Ms. Ogata, even, who was the then-president of the UNHCR in Geneva. We toured the entire refugee camp in Gasinci. She was quite pleased to see what we were doing and the way we were doing it. She talked to various people we met on the way. She was quite grateful to me for everything we did. She said, I admire you, you are doing this far better than many other countries. We also went to Zagreb together, where I took her to the refugee settlements in Kruge, in Spansko, and elsewhere. As for Obonjan, so that everyone would know what we are talking about, it is a beautiful island close to Sibenik. On that island, before that war, there were scouts who would spend summers there. The island had infrastructure. There were also youth meetings, international meetings there, and the name of the island in popular terms was the island of youth. When the refugee crisis occurred we asked the Ministry of Tourism and the city of Sibenik, in whose territory the island is, to rent it to us. On the island we accommodated refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were Muslims, but there were some Croats among them as well, as well as the Roma, Serbs, basically all ethnicities of the former Yugoslavia. First we accommodated a certain number of refugees on the premises that existed there, in the buildings that were there. But as the number of refugees grew, for the first time there we began using tents, as we did in Split and Stobrec for a short while until we were able to come up with a different solution. People do not like staying in tents, it is quite understandable. As regards Obonjan, I was there on two or three occasions to visit, especially at the outset when my colleague, who is an attorney, his name is Miso Hribar, organized the accommodation there. I found no reason for dissatisfaction personally. Of course people wanted more and better food, but they would also fish and grill it or to get by in different ways. As far as I know, nobody ever went hungry on that island. Thank God there was enough food. Of course there wasn't food to waste, although food was wasted, not in that centre but in a different centre I arrived there with an international delegation we came across piles of food that had been wasted. That is understandable as well. Obonjan had a doctor, an out-patient clinic, a dentist, a mosque, an extra-territorial school, it had everything. There was also a ferry at the disposal of the refugees, for example, for situations which required other assistance, say, women in labour or people in need of medical -- urgent medical assistance, then they would be transferred to Sibenik by that ferry since it took it only about 20 to 30 minutes to arrive there. In that regard Obonjan was covered as well. There were also doctors coming from abroad who served as volunteers. There was also a young French NGO, they worked with children and the youth. Anyone with good intentions was free to come and assist, of course after gaining our permission. We wanted to know who was going to the centres and with what intentions. This is what I can tell you about Obonjan in short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever receive any complaints from, say, the UNHCR that your office or the Government of the Republic of Croatia was deliberately discriminating against the Muslims that were staying either in Gasinci or this particular island, Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: No. I never received any express complaints; quite to the contrary. We cooperated on resolving certain problems which occurred from time to time. For the most part it had to do with food and health care. It was the UNHCR which would lend a hand in such cases and would help in resolving the issues. It is understandable that there may have been complaints. People complain in peacetimes, in towns and villages. There are demonstrations such as the ones that were in Zagreb, because on occasion the conditions there are not satisfactory. Of course there was a slight degree of dissatisfaction; however, in those circumstances we couldn't give more than we were able to. We were quite limited in terms of resources but there was never any bad faith or lack of will to give the refugees what they were due.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I was intentionally waiting, Your Honour, just to see if Mr. Karnavas might have a follow-up question because I know last week he suggested that I was on my feet too quickly. As the Chamber knows, the question of dates and time, timing is quite critical to the case and something that happened in 1992 or 1995 is quite different than what happened in 1993. And I wonder if -- I wonder if Mr. Karnavas could assist us with the particular dates of the visits to Obonjan and Gasinci, if the witness can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly. And I appreciate that intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We are going to go through all these documents, but could you tell us when you visited those facilities, those centres?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Today, 15 years later, it is difficult for me to recall specific dates. I know I was on the island of Obonjan when the refugee centre was being set up; it was sometime in 1992. I also visited it on one other occasion when Obonjan became overcrowded with the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It may have been in the first half of 1993. I am certain I visited Obonjan twice at least. As far as Gasinci go, I was there more frequently because some delegations were particularly interested in it, diplomatic delegations, humanitarian delegations, and I mentioned Mrs. Sadako Ogata, whom I took there. I also took there some German ministers and ministers from other countries. I went there with Muslims, that is to say the Arabic humanitarian organizations as well as the German Caritas and other European humanitarian organizations and people who wanted to provide assistance to Gasinci in particular. For example, Germans and Danes offered to build bungalows there so that the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina would have satisfactory accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. We're going to get into these documents, we've seen them before, but there's been an exchange of documents where Azra Krajsek and to some extent Turkovic, who was the ambassador at the time, was sending letters to you. And of course we're going to go through them in detail. But could you please tell us whether they ever came to your office, in particular Azra Krajsek who was, as we will see, was writing to her ministry without copying you -- at least that's what's indicated in the letters. Did she ever come to your office and concretely explain to you what the problems were in either Gasinci or Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Ms. Azra Krajsek came to Zagreb as an attache of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian embassy, either in early 1993 or towards the end of 1992, I don't know precisely. I do believe, however, that it was in March 1993, we stayed there until January or February 1994 or perhaps a month or two longer. She came to the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees on several occasions. Our relations were good. We would usually discuss the problems in Gasinci and Obonjan. She seemed to have focused particularly on those two refugee centres. She wasn't very much interested in many other refugee centres where there were many Muslims and Croats. I don't know why she exhibited such interest in those two particular ones. Well, they may have been specific in some regards and that could explain that. She never came to me with specific problems or complaints of significant degree. She usually came with the type of problems which were understandable for such situation in which we had centres with 3, 4, 5.000 people. There were problems with the supply. There were differences among the people living there. There were people who came from the urban setting, then there were others who came from the country-side, their mentality was different and it was difficult to harmonize all that. I believe she also found herself in such situations where she listened to individuals. I also came across such individuals who were always dissatisfied. Those people came from among the refugees as well as from among the Croatian citizens. I was in a hotel in Trogir where the Croatian citizens there told us that we are eating bread that is three days old and the soup is bad, the food is bad, and I went there to check their kitchen. I came there unannounced, and to my opinion it was a good kitchen, a kitchen which would satisfy the need of a lower-quality hotel. There were also situations in which cooks were professionals and educated, but quite often refugees would assist as well in the kitchen. In Gasinci, unfortunately, there was a food poisoning once and the cook himself was poisoned alongside his two assistants but no one else was. That could happen in Zagreb today or in any of the tourist resorts during the summer. We tried to deal with such things right away. We would go there immediately and deal with it. I had no particular problems with Azra Krajsek or any other people, at least she was never too outspoken about it. She could not know of all the instructions I had sent to the various regional offices and she may not have been fully acquainted with the situation. When such problems would occur I would call Bisera Turkovic and Azra Krajsek as well as Tadic and Raguz and we would sit down and discuss things. For example, on the 11th of April, 1993, we discussed the issue for three hours. The issue discussed then was the issue of abolishing refugee status and those refugees which were unable to return to their homes did not see their status abolished at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Karnavas asked you to speak about the UNHCR, you talked about the ambassadors, you talked about ministers including the German minister. Listening to you the following question comes to my mind. What about the Catholic church, your own hierarchy, and the Bishop in Zagreb and up to the Holy See in Rome, were they following the humanitarian situation very closely, the situation of local refugees because there were organizations such as Caritas on site? Was the Catholic church involved in these operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is good that you put this question since it needs to be clarified as well. The Catholic church in Croatia does have it Caritas organization which after the democratic changes developed significantly. It assisted greatly the displaced persons and refugees. Had it not been for the Caritas it would have been very difficult to accommodate all displaced persons and feed all the refugees. I know what I'm talking about, I know what the Caritas was doing, and I particularly did not go into that since I wanted to avoid being subjective or biassed. However, I can freely say that the Caritas did a lot. Priests appealed to their flock to provide assistance. They distributed food to refugees and they housed many refugees and displaced persons. They were on good terms and there was never an incident which may have taken place between a Catholic priest and a Muslim. All Muslims were received well and they received the same assistance. However, I must say that the Merhamet did not always act the same way, but I'd rather not go into any further discussion concerning the Merhamet. There were many Muslims and I do understand that the Merhamet took care only of the Muslims and not the Catholic population; that is understandable, however. We were sufficiently well organized to be able to assist the displaced persons of Catholic belief or affiliation. The church always assisted through its hierarchical system. I also need to mention the Monsignor Vladimir Stankovic who was the director of the Caritas was also a member of the administrative board of our office alongside the director of the Croatian Red Cross as well as two people from the parliament and another two people from the government itself. He was in the administrative board of the office acting on behalf of the Catholic church and the Caritas. The Caritas was directly involved and was familiar with the needs. The Caritas in Croatia received a lot of help from the German and US Caritas. In Zagreb there was even an office of the American -- well, I don't know exactly what the name of the office was, but they were in charge of taking care of displaced persons and refugees. The Italian Caritas had its office in Zagreb, it was Antonietta, a nun who toured such people, in particular Muslims. Although a nun, she was fascinated with Muslims and she gladly assisted them in terms of food, money, she was involved in some construction as well. As far as that goes, there were no divisions, no tension. Every now and then things might happen as everywhere, but in general I was quite pleased to see how quickly people reacted to assist and with the solidarity I encountered at the time. Today in Croatia you cannot see any such solidarity, any more such as the one that was in place during the war until 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in a nutshell was Rome perfectly informed of the situation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were informed. I was visited, or rather, the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees was visited by a representative of the Holy See who came to Zagreb. He visited the office and asked me how we were dealing with accommodating refugees and displaced persons, whether there were any religious tensions, and so on. Right now his last name eludes me. He was the secretary of state of the Holy See. I also was visited by representatives of the Catholic church in Germany, on one occasion several Bishops. I know there was the assistant Bishop of Munster, who used to be a school colleague of mine in Rome, Monsignor Foss came to see us, so I can say that we did receive support. Cardinal Franjo Kuharic did not visit refugee centres and nobody expected him to because of all his other duties, but he gave me a great deal of support and he always told me I had to work honourably and honestly, with decency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Brussels, was Brussels informed? That's where the EU -- EC was, were they informed because they were also assisting financially?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were very well informed and they join in the SETF, a special programme of the European community of providing supplies to refugees and displaced persons, supplies of food, was active. SETF was active almost throughout the refugee and displaced persons crisis. That's precisely why we had to make lists, why we had to take censuses, because the European Community and the UNHCR had to know exactly how many displaced persons and refugees we had and how many there were, in what locations, so that they could provide assistance. We had good cooperation with the SETF to ensure that food always reached a particular location. We didn't want it to get lost on the way from the warehouse to the refugee centre and be distributed to somebody else. For that reason, there was a commission organized by the SETF, the European Community, and our office jointly, which had the right to stop every truck along the road and follow it to the refugee centre that was its destination, where food had to be distributed. This was a way to avoid manipulation, for example, the selling of food and so on, because we did hear complaints that humanitarian aid was being sold on the markets. But this did not occur to such a large extent that we could trace it to some high-level manipulation. What did happen was that sometimes a refugee would get a can of food and they would take it along to the market and sell it in order to get some cash, but these were minor incidents. Some people did this in order to get some cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. And what about Geneva, was Geneva informed?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were thoroughly informed, both through the UNHCR which was in constant contact with Geneva with Madam Ogata, and I also attended several meetings in Geneva. I also attended a meeting of the ICRC, Mrs. -- Sommaruga. On two occasions I was in Geneva together with Mrs. Ogata. On one occasion this had to do with abolishing refugee status so that the humanitarian organizations and the ICRC and the UNHCR and all the ones that have their headquarters in Geneva were well informed of the refugee and displaced person crisis in the Republic of Croatia. I keep stressing our good relations within the UNHCR and how we received help from them, but this help was 10 per cent of our overall needs. However, even 10 per cent is a lot in the situation we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I know you've provided me with this report that you wrote: "My work at the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees," is 1D 02921, and in it you describe various meetings and personalities that you met Mazowiecki, O'Shay, Ogata, without going into it, would it be fair to say that in this report here, this report of yours, you cover the contacts that you had with the international community concerning your activities during the period of 1991 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, Mr. Karnavas, my secretary kept a log-book and she kept my agenda, and when I left the office my secretary gave it to me. I didn't throw it away, I kept it. I didn't think I would ever need it, but now is the time to look into my agenda and then we can see what we were doing and how we were doing it at the time. Of course it's not a detailed diary. There were many delegations who visited who are not mentioned here. There were many meetings not mentioned here, but still what is really important is noted down and you can see what -- well, people called it my office. It was the government office actually. But you can see what number of delegations we received. On the average it was five delegations a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: So that's as far as this document is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to move rather quickly. I just have a couple of quick areas to touch on before we go into the documents. First of all, I would like to know whether your office was issuing any guarantees and whether it had the right to issue any guarantees to third countries. In other words, someone coming in from Bosnia-Herzegovina, could your office issue a guarantee for that person to, say, go to Germany or Switzerland or Turkey and did that occur?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Persons who went to third countries had to receive guarantees from those third countries, not from us. The -- what refugees received from the Office for Displaced persons And Refugees was that they could enter the Republic of Croatia and be accommodated as refugees and displaced persons. Further, those refugees who were under the protection of UNHCR and who went to third countries, we could issue them with a transit visa. It wasn't a real transit visa. It was a document confirming that with the permission of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees persons under the protection of the UNHCR who intend to go to a third country may stay in the Republic of Croatia in the interim, in the meantime, while they are waiting to go to the third country and they needed this document so that they could show it if there was a police check or something and it had political weight. So it would provide security or protection to the person who held it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, to your knowledge and your recollection, did you ever recall a situation where some refugees went to a third country of their own volition, presumably with a guarantee provided by that country that they would receive them; and then those refugees wished to return to Croatia as refugees?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. The reasons were different. Sometimes refugees wanted to go back because they thought the accommodation in Croatia was better than the accommodation they got in Germany or some other country, and those persons actually said that in the letters they wrote to us. We always received those persons back without question because it was our duty as the first neighbouring country. We then gave those persons refugee status, accommodated them in refugee centre or a centre for displaced persons, and they could stay there for as long as they were unable to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina or until such time as the conditions were created for their return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were instances where the Bosnian embassy accommodated a group of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Turkey. I received several telephone calls from these Bosnian refugees saying they wanted to go back to Croatia because they said it was better in Croatia than in Turkey. They said Croatia was doing a better job accommodating refugees than Turkey was. They were somewhere west of Istanbul near the border with Bulgaria. They complained they weren't getting enough food. They complained that they were accommodated in tents and so on. Well, it's understandable because that country also had numerous refugees. And Mr. Demeril told me so himself, and a minister of his when we visited Stobrec in Split where there were refugees of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were of Bosniak-Muslim ethnicity, and they were complaining they wanted this and they wanted that, and the minister said to me, Well, we're having the same problems. In Turkey people are also saying they want this and they want. A refugee is a refugee. These are people who are under stress, who are wounded, they are people who have seen other people killed. A refugee is not happy even when you put him up in a hotel long term. These are people who had suffered psychological injuries, and if somebody went around Gasinci and Obonjan and listened to someone speaking, they would have to know whether that person was under stress, whether that person had had some kind of psychological trauma, or whether they were objective or subjective, and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minor related question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just follow-up on this, Mr. President, before you pose your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question is you had indicated some Bosnians, I think that was the way you termed it, went to Turkey and now were calling you. Do you know whether they were Croats or Muslim or both? That's question number one. And number two is: What did you do? Did you say, Stay there because we have already enough of you, or did you bring them back?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims because the Bosnian embassy, as a rule, did not look after Croat refugees. They always said, Well, that's for the Republic of Croatia to take care of. I'm saying that as a rule because they did have goodwill towards others and other refugees. But in this particular case they were Muslims and the Bosnian embassy wanted to put them up in Turkey with the best of intentions in the conviction that they would be better off there. However, these people called me up on the telephone and said they were not better off there. Allow me to say that even Israel sent a representative to me and they offered to receive 200 refugees, Muslim refugees, from Bosnia-Herzegovina. They said, We want Muslims, you see, we are Israelis, we have tensions with Palestinians, with Muslims, and we want to show that we care about Muslims in a country where they are under threat in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So about 200 of them went to Israel and they were accommodated in Jerusalem, and it was very hard to find them. In Split we went around the centres asking who wanted to go to Israel and we could barely get together 150 of them. They weren't very enthusiastic. I visited them in 1993 or 1994 when I was attending a congress in Jerusalem on the subject of genocide. On that occasion I visited these people. They were mostly rather young because the elderly really didn't want to fly to Tel-Aviv and Jerusalem, and they weren't very happy, they weren't very satisfied. Because, you know, people always think it's best to be at home, and when you're close to Bosnia you feel better than when you are far from Bosnia. There is a poem in our language: The sun of a foreign sky will never keep you as warm as the sun in your own land. I hope the interpreters understand that. The poet was Aleksa Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Concretely if you could answer my question, when they called and they wanted to come back from Turkey, did you receive them, did the Republic of Croatia receive these refugees?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: My answer to those persons was: If you succeed in organizing transport to Croatia, we'll receive you. So I said, Well, call the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they transported you there so they may be able to transport you back because otherwise we would be in a quandary. We couldn't go and interfere in something that the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina had tried to resolve. So that looking back now I can't really remember how the story ended, but as for countries like Slovenia, Germany, and so on people did come back because it was easier to travel back to Croatia and they continued being in Croatia as refugees until they went back to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, speaking of returning, and this is sort of the last topic before we get to the documents. With respect to returning refugees from Croatia, say, back to Bosnia-Herzegovina - in other words, where they lose their status - can you please explain to us what the procedure was in general and we're mostly concerned to know whether the Republic of Croatia deliberately revoked someone's status as a refugee and deported them back to Bosnia-Herzegovina, putting them into harm's way? And I'm speaking of a period of say in 1994, 1995, late 1993, that's what I'm speaking of.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees never forced anyone to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know very well that we did have some problems regarding the revoking of refugee status and the revoking of displaced persons status. Our stand point was the same in both cases, both displaced persons and refugees. And just as Slovenia, Germany, Denmark, and other countries had done who sent our refugees back from those countries, as soon as the conditions were in place for persons who had been expelled to be able to go back we sent them back right away in Osijek in Croatia, for example, or remember when Western Slavonia was liberated, all our displaced persons went to their destroyed houses in eastern Slavonia and then with the help of the state they rebuilt their houses and started farming their land and tried to heal the wounds of the four-year-long occupation. And just as today Serbs are going back to Croatia from which they had fled so that as we were sending back our own citizens to the places they had fled from when the situation quietened down, we did the same with refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. As soon as an area of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was safe from war and the threat of war, the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees issued a decree revoking refugee status so that people could go back. And the territories, the towns and places, were clearly designated to which they could go back. So we never sent them back just anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but to precisely designated places. As the head of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, I issued instructions to the regional offices that they could revoke refugee status only for those refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina who could go back, whose houses had not been destroyed, who were not in peril in the areas where they had to go back, who were not sick, whose children were in school. So my instructions were quite clear. There were instances where these refugees could not be sent back. There was some lack of clarity there in their office and in the regional offices, which is why Bisera Turkovic, Azra Krajsek, Tadic, Raguz and I met and we discussed the issue and agreed. And then again I sent instructions to all the regional offices and social welfare centres as to how they were to proceed, what refugees had to be sent back, what refugees must not be sent back, what refugees had to have their status prolonged, extended. And after that there were no more tensions because you can always solve everything by talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you did indicate that there were refugees that had left from Croatia and had gone to places like Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Belgium, and what have you. Were you -- did the Republic of Croatia ever come under any pressure at any time to take back its refugees, irrespective of whether they were -- they had originated from Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: No. Those people simply came back to Croatia. Many of them didn't even ask our office whether they were allowed to go back or not. They simply came back to Croatia, and then they reported. They knew to whom they should report, to the office for displaced persons and refugees or a regional office, and they were given refugee or displaced persons status, as the case may be, and that was constantly our practice which never changed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- did there ever come a time when you had to sign an agreement, negotiate an agreement with Germany and others because Germany wanted refugees out of Germany and back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Germany was very anxious for Croatian refugees to go back to Croatia, regardless of whether they were originally Croatian citizens or Bosnian refugees who had a Croatian passport. Germany treated all such refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were in Germany as Croat citizens, and they said, Please take them back. You have given them passports so now take them back, and of course we did. Bosnian Catholics, Croats, and Bosnian Muslims had such passports. Many Muslims were issued with Croatian passports. At that time it was enough for a Muslim from Bosnia-Herzegovina to show the department in the Ministry of the Interior any document, a driving licence, a school certificate, which said that he had declared himself to be a Croat at some time and ipso facto he had the right to a Croatian certificate of citizenship and Croatian documents. There were in 1992 very many such Muslims from Bosnia who went to Denmark, Sweden, Germany, above all, with Croatian passports. And then when the Germans had had enough and when they realized they couldn't have 200.000 refugees from Croatia because these people's point of departure to Germany was Croatia, so in their eyes they didn't care whether these were Croats or Bosniaks. And I went to Germany to talk to Mr. Kanther the German minister and other responsible persons -- the minister of the interior, that is, and I signed a document with them on the return of all Croat refugees to Croatia. This was an agreement on gradual organized return to all liberated places in the Republic of Croatia. And we had to give them a list as to what places were now free of war and what places were not. And they had that list. And that was what guided us when we were sending refugees back to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but by that time I had already left the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees and my colleague, Damir Zoric, continued, but we had a good precedent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Just to follow up. For instance, on the concerns from Germany, looking at the documents I realized that on the 12th of July, 1993, at 11.45 until 1.00 you received Dr. Angela Merkel. Do you remember why you met with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Angela Merkel arrived just as many others. At the time she did not have the function that she has today nor was her importance the same as it is today. She arrived as a member of the Christian Social Union, I believe that that was her party, and she was interested in our treatment of Muslims. Obviously she had heard some things, read some things, in the media. Because, let's admit it, at the time we were accused from all sides, either rightfully or wrongfully, that we did make some differences. She asked me why we made a difference, and I said, Mrs. Merkel, it's not us that we make any differences. We do not treat Muslims any differently than we do Catholics from Bosnia. They're all refugees to us. To me they were all refugees. But we do have problems. Don't have you have them in Germany? Don't you have any problems with the Turks? And Merkel says, Well, that's our problem. And I said, Well, this is ours. I was a bit harsh with Merkel, I must admit, because she had arrived from a different situation and she could speak about those problems differently than I could because I was faced with those problems every day, day in day out, I had to deal with them as best as I could. Croatia was so much more different than Germany. Germany was rich and well developed. We provided what we could under the circumstances, but nobody received milk and honey, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to take a break now unless you have a question, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question because I just want to make sure that the entire Bench is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the Republic of Croatia make a distinction when it came to providing aid, when it came to providing assistance, when it came to providing education, when it came to providing health care, did it make a distinction between refugees that were Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Catholics be they or Muslims, did they make a distinction? Because we have Merkel, but I want to make sure that we're very clear on this point.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: The Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons never made any distinctions whatsoever. If anybody did outside the office, if they made any distinctions, then you should ask them. But the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons, its regional offices, there were 21 of them, and all the centres for social welfare never made any distinctions between the refugees. Under the given situation, under the given circumstances, we treated everybody the same. We were an office for refugees not an office for refugee Croats or refugee Muslims. They were all refugees to us and we did not have any right to treat ones differently than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I invite the Bench if they have questions on this; otherwise, we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to take the break. We'll resume around 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the hearing is resumed. Judge Prandler has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't want to interrupt you, Mr. Karnavas, before the break. But now since you have merely dealt with the contacts with internationals and also some states concerned, I would like to refer to the document I believe that you are also going to ask the witness about the documents you are going to submit, a document which is in binder 2 and the number has already been mentioned today several times, 1D 02921, 2921, and it is actually the very submission or report of the witness, Dr. Rebic, entitled: "My work at the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees." So it is again just to have -- helping the refugee. It is in binder number 2 and the number is 2921. So in that report of yours you make a reference to, among other things, your visit to Hungary on page 4 and I do not want to hide that I am Hungarian, but of course I speak not in my capacity as Hungarian but as a independent Judge, but I am also pleased to read that you found that there was a lot of help offered by Hungary during that time, and I can re-confirm that working at that time in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Hungary. And also in -- on page 4 you mentioned that you met UNHCR representatives together with at that time the minister of interior, Mr. Petar Buros [phoen], and the minister of foreign affairs, Mr. Geza Jesenski, and others. Now here there is one small issue which I would like to raise that during this very first part of this sitting and hearing you have mentioned that only 2.500 refugees remained in Hungary, but I believe the correct number is that -- when you mentioned that out of that number, that is the number coming from Croatia and other countries, only out of that number 2.500 returned to Croatia, so not remained but returned I believe it is the correct interpretation of those numbers. Now, in the next paragraph you mention, and you mentioned this before, that together with vice-president Mato Granic you had been to Geneva to visit the International Red Cross, read ICRC and not IRC and the High Commissioner for refugees. And you mentioned there that you met there Mr. Cornelius Sommaruga, then president of the ICRC, and visited Ms. Sadako Ogata. Now, of course I mean, it is my question that Hungary arranged at that time several visits by President Sommaruga, among other things, to try to have talks which were held in Hungary at that time between the relevant representatives of Croatia and Serbia at that time at that time the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And just for the very important issue for the exchange of prisoners of war and of course of the other detainees. So I would like to ask you if your office has also been -- has it also been involved with the exchange of persons having a POW status and that of the displaced persons and other detainees between the countries concerned, i.e., between Croatia and then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, otherwise Serbia? So it is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I'd like to use this opportunity to thank you as a Hungarian and to thank Hungary for everything it did for Croatia, not only to assist with the refugee and displaced persons crisis but also to thank you for the very good relations between Hungary and Croatia in general. We have no unresolved issues between the two countries. As regards your question, I was indirectly involved in it. When I say that I mean to say that for the prisoners, Croatian prisoners that were exchanged, or rather, released by the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, were subsequently taken care of our Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees and were given the status of displaced persons. If I'm not mistaken, there were 3 or 400 of them. I was tasked with receiving them, organizing a meal, and accommodation for them. I remember it well. It took place on the 14th of August, just before the Assumption of Our Lady religious holiday, and I ascribed that to the blessed Virgin Mary, and to my mind it was a miracle since it took place just the evening before our great religious holiday. It is another topic that we will probably touch upon later and I am probably anticipating, but I just wanted to say something that has to do with those who were transferred from Bosnia-Herzegovina having been prisoners before that time. We were received in the Republic of Croatia as refugees; that is to say, we awarded them refugee status. The transfer itself was done by the UNHCR. The UNHCR had promised them to leave to a third country and they only requested transit permits from our office. They asked for the refugees to remain in Croatia in the interim while the UNHCR was working on the issue. I did, therefore, participate in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, with respect to Hungary, we find that on the 19th of March you went to Hungary to visit a number of camps, and in your report I realize that there is an office very similar to yours. There is an office in charge of displaced persons and refugees, apparently it's headed by Mr. Markus [phoen] and Mr. Molnaj [phoen]. You went to a number of camps with these two individuals and you encouraged people to go home, to go back home. What I find interesting here is to see that your office existed also in another country, in Hungary. Was it also the case in Slovenia and was it also the case in Germany? Did they have an Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees working along similar lines as yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me clarify one thing first. The Office for Displaced Persons in Hungary was not our office, it was an office of the Hungarian government. It was organized along the same lines and following the same principles as ours was. Slovenia had an office like that as well as part of their Ministry of Foreign Affairs. They had an Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. We had permanent contact with them as well much like we did with the Hungarian office. As for Mr. Markus and Molnaj, I came to visit them on other two or three occasions and we visited the centres together, Atac [phoen] and Segacut [phoen] where our refugees were accommodated. The accommodation was satisfactory. They had no particular complaints. The only one being that they wanted to go home as early as possible, it was a wish of theirs. They returned once the area around Osijek had been liberated, when the threat was removed. It was then that the number of our refugees reduced drastically, from some 30.000 to 2 or 3.000 that were left. Those who were unable to go back because they hailed from Vukovar which was occupied. Those people remained in Hungary for quite some time. During their stay in Hungary, they received food, health care, and everything prescribed under the law that is required by such offices. I might also mention that on the 25th of March of that same year, 1992, in Zagreb in the inter-continental, which is today the Westin, we held a tripartite meeting. You mentioned Mr. Molnaj from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in charge of humanitarian issues. We discussed the whole day how to help and accommodate refugees and displaced persons. Hungary also came to our assistance on that occasion particularly. Unfortunately, such tripartite meetings did not take place afterwards. The humanitarian aid arriving from the neighbouring countries was done more or less on an ad hoc basis and somewhat chaotically. But upon the Croatian and Hungarian initiative to meet with the UNHCR, that meeting took place and it showed itself to be quite useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last very quick question. We know, because last -- the witness told us so last week and because we saw a number of documents with -- in line with this that there were more than 1.8 million refugees in your country. And reading these documents we find that these refugees went to Germany, Hungary, and then further on to the US or to Canada. This was a major problem. Don't you think that it should have been dealt with as a priority by the UNHCR and that you yourself should have just helped this international action, considering the scale of the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the beginning of the war we did not have a UNHCR office in Croatia, in Zagreb. There was a UNHCR representative who was still in Belgrade at the time, and he could do nothing for our displaced persons and refugees who had to flee and go to third countries throughout 1991 and beginning of 1992. A UNHCR office was founded in Zagreb as late as January or February 1992. First there was Mr. Mendeluce. He arrived there with a single set of clothes because he managed to flee Sarajevo and the shelling there. He was followed by Mr. Comkulato and it was she who had the permission of Geneva to establish a UNHCR office in Croatia. As of January, that is to say on the 15th of January, 1992, Croatia was internationally recognised. It was as late as the 15th of January. That is when Croatia was internationally recognised. After that -- the UNHCR office was founded in Croatia. After that, the UNHCR did take part in these issues, however it was gradual. I must say here that thank God in January 1992 there were no more combat activities in the free territory of Croatia. That meant that all our refugees from Slovenia, Hungary, and Austria returned to, for example, Osijek, Karlovac, Sisak, Varazdin, and Zagreb itself because people fled all those cities, they went anywhere to save their hides. You must remember that Zagreb itself was shelled. I very much wanted to go back to Zagreb in September 1991, but the first night I spent there I was forced to spend it in a cellar. Of course everyone wants to go back to their country even if there is shelling and that was the situation in the field. Our people truly wanted to go back to their homeland, and as soon as it was free of the threat of war they came back. The 1.800.000 was the number that existed in a certain particular moment in time, in December 1991. However, as early as January 1992 a great deal of those Croatian refugees returned to Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Unless there are any other questions, I'm going to go right into the documents. And, Your Honours, I had to make some re-arrangements of the documents so they're not quite in the order of which I will be dealing in your binders. I'll be referring to the numbers but they're not in the exact order because I'm trying to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to start with binder 1. Binder 1 for you, Dr. Rebic, if we could get some assistance. Just -- and I'm going to be asking your -- I'm going to be asking Dr. Rebic to ever be so kind to give me short answers, short, so that we can go through these documents. Nothing causes me more anxiety than the time spent going through documents.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much. You can break me always.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just for some technical matters to get out of the way. If you look at 1D 02584, 1D 02584, that's the very first document in your binder, sir, we see that this is a decision appointing you as the Office of the Displaced Persons and Refugees 11 December -- it says 1891 but obviously that must be a mistake, right, it must be 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: But the datum is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: The datum 1891 I see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: It should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it's based on this document that you became the head?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we look at the next document 1D 02632, we see that this is a decision to relieve you -- to relieve of duty the head of Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, Dr. Adalbert Rebic, 2 February 1996. This must have been -- this is the document that relieved you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. And again, in the Catholic church it is another holiday concerning the blessed Virgin Mary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it this was sort of a happy day for you because you wanted to get back to your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If we -- now I want to go to the -- the next section will be dealing with a few documents related to the laws, the legislation that was -- that we've looked at last week. But again I just want to make some -- get some confirmation. First document is 1D 02632, 2632. We see here it's a decree on establishing the Office for Refugees of the Republic of Croatia, and there's a date of 30 August 1991. Were you familiar with -- is this the decree --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [In English] It is 23 [Interpretation] 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is 2623.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [In English] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I could have this -- okay. And are you familiar with this decree?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes and no because this -- [Interpretation] Excuse me. This decree preceded the founding of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. This was a decree dealing with the establishment of an interim office that was supposed to deal with the refugees and displaced persons. As you can see it is the 30th of August, 1991, whereas the office was formed subsequently by another decree. This was an interim one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if we look at 1D 02637, 2637, and we see it's dated 22 November 1991. This is a decree of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It is a decree pursuant to which the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees was founded as part of the Government of the Republic of Croatia. I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was it based on this decree that your office was operating on?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: We based our activities on this decree and no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document and I'm going to ask you to comment slightly on this, it's 1D 02634, 2634, we see it's 11 December 1991 and this is a decision to appoint president, deputy president, and members of the steering council of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. Of course I believe you did make a comment earlier about one of the individuals on this steering council, but very briefly could you please tell us what was this steering council and how was it related to what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the steering committee was a supervisory body in charge of our Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees; that is to say, they supervised the work of the office. The members of the committee met every two or three months or, if need be, more frequently if there was a problem at hand. The committee was comprised of Bernardo Jurlina, who was the minister for social welfare and family issues. It took care of the displaced persons and refugees on behalf of the office; however, since the number of refugees and displaced persons was too great for the ministry to deal with because by that time the numbering went over 300.000, the government established a separate office. Then there was Mr. Skrabalo who was in charge of cooperation between the World Health Organization and the Republic of Croatia. He is a physician by vocation. The third member was Monsignor Vladimir Stankovic, director of the Caritas of the Bishop conference. He was also in charge of the Croatian pastoral mission abroad. His purview was over all priests working outside of Croatia. Most of them were in Germany. Then there was Dr. Javornik, who was the general secretary of the Croatian Red Cross. He assisted the work in terms of accommodation greatly. Then there was Primarius Dr. Kostovic, who is a physician and a professor at the medical school. There was Dr. Kutle and Ms. Turic who were there on behalf of the parliament of the Republic of Croatia. As you can see from the composition all these people were professionals, competent and responsible people overseeing the work of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was this steering council in existence throughout the period while you were head of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, it's 1D 02588, 2588. We see that this is a decree that's dated 27 October 1992. It's a decree on status of displaced persons and refugees. And my first question is: Are you familiar with this decree; and if so, how so?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this decree. In relation to the first decree promulgated a year earlier, it became law because the Croatian parliament ratified it and it is signed here by the deputy prime minister Ivan Milas. This made the decree a law of the Republic of Croatia, and the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees had to act under that law. It doesn't differ very much from the previous decree. There are just a few minor changes in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at -- was it based on this decree on the status of displaced persons and refugees that your office determined the status of whether somebody could enjoy the status of being a displaced person or refugee and the benefits that went with that status?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: It was according to this decree that we established a person's status.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again 1D 02635, here we see that there is an amendment to the decree of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, and were you familiar with this document? This refers to the decree establishing your office as opposed to the other one, which was the status?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes [Interpretation] Yes. I am extremely familiar with this. This decree better defines what departments should be part of the office for care and organized accommodation, for the organized return, that's one department, then the next one is of finance, the third is department for gathering transport and distribution of humanitarian aid, then there's the department for cooperation with international humanitarian organizations, the department for social adaptations, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 02638, we see this is a decision now, it's dated 6 October 1993 -- it's a law, I'm sorry, it's a law.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, it's the law, I apologise. And were you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. It was signed by the president of the Republic of Croatia because when he signs a law it enters into force in the Republic of Croatia, and I was bound by this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was it based on this law that you determined the status of an individual, whether he qualified for benefits and the status of being either a displaced person or a refugee?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, we talked a little bit earlier about education and about the rights that were afforded to individuals. If we could just for purposes of an example look at 1D 02610, and I will ask you to comment on this, 2610. This is dated January 12th, 1994. We see at the bottom -- we see at the bottom that your name is mentioned. Now, if we look at the original version or copy of the original, that is your signature, is it not, Dr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, it is my signature. It's in good order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please very briefly explain the contents of this particular document since you were the author.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: The Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina requested from us through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to provide them with precise data on the number of children attending the regular school programme. Of course I forwarded this document to the Ministry of Culture and Education, asking them to provide this information to the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with a copy or with copies to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and to me. And this document shows that in the Republic of Croatia refugees did have the possibility of schooling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. May I ask, why was it that you needed to ask the -- another ministry for that data? Why was it that your office, the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees, did not have that data readily available?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Because it was the Ministry of Culture and Education that was in charge of schooling, and only it could provide precise information on those attending school in the Republic of Croatia. This was not within the remit of the ODPR, the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just a technical question that might be on the Judges' mind. What about for extra-territorial schools, where would that data be? Or did this ministry also have data concerning pupils that were attending extra-territorial schools that were established either for Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina or Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: With respect to those attending extra-territorial primary schools in refugee centres, it was also the Ministry of Culture and Education that was in charge if those refugee centres were on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Mostly, however, the refugee centres and the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina relied on information coming from the refugee centres because there were teachers there who issued school certificates at the end of the academic year, and of course these certificates had to be recognised by the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why in the documents they sent to me and in my conversations with them extra-territorial schools were frequently mentioned. They functioned well in some places, worse in others, they were well-structured in some places, less-well-structured in others, and it all depended on the people we were working with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally just one last issue to make sure that we are on the same page, if we could look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is not in the binders, Your Honour, but it's in the e-court system, it's 4D 01232.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't have it, it's not in your binder, but it should pop up on the screen. Dr. Rebic, Dr. Rebic, it should pop up on your screen. This was a document that was shown last week. It's the Law on Movement and Stay of Foreigners.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 28 June 1991, and could you please tell us whether this particular law applied to the refugees coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this law did not apply to refugees from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. First of all, this law was promulgated in Zagreb on the 28th of June, 1991, before there were any refugees from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were only displaced, or rather, there were refugees from Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. It was the other way around. Because at that time the JNA had not yet perpetrated aggression there. So this law did not concern those who were coming from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; it was -- it pertained to those coming from other countries such as Greece, Bulgaria, where they came even from Pakistan. We had cases where among the refugees in Croatia in 1991 there were refugees from far-away countries. Excuse me, I misspoke. The date is the 28th of June -- no, no, no, it's all right. I didn't misspeak. I didn't misspeak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when they refer to foreigners, they're not referring to - if I understand you correctly - they're not referring to citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as far as -- just to make sure, your office was not -- your office in granting status --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: It did not act pursuant to this law, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, we're going to move on to another area, and we're going to be looking at 1D 02629, if you could find that, that's the next document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again I apologise to Your Honours for not having them in the sequential order. We had to re-arrange this at the last moment. I wish I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's the last of binder 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's the last of binder 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to be going through a series of reports, and let me ask this question before we get to this document. As part of your job being the head of the office, were you obliged to keep statistics and make reports?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Karnavas, very frequently and very exhaustively and very professionally because we sent that information and those statistic to the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on this particular document, 1D 02629, we see this is a survey and at the bottom we see who conducted the survey. Is it fair to say that your office did not conduct this survey; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: No, it was not our office that conducted the survey. It was the PULS agency which still exists in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we turn to page 3, if we turn to page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, could the witness perhaps tell us what is behind this word, pulse, what does it mean, you said it is the PULS, that is still here to be found. What is the PULS agency, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the name of an agency conducting polls, public opinion polls. It takes its names according to a person's pulse, a person's heart beat.
