So it should be understood in the medical sense, pulse. Whether they really felt the pulse of the people correctly every time, that's a different question; but they are always very active whenever we have elections for a new parliament or a new president, they do opinion polls today still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now if we look at page 3 at the bottom we note that your office was involved to the extent of providing data. It says: "All necessary permissions and recommendations for implementation of the research have been obtained from Mr. Adalbert Rebic."

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit about what was it that you did that enabled PULS, PULS agency, to conduct this particular survey?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: The PULS agency first needed permission from the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees to conduct their opinion poll, the opinions of individual refugees, displaced persons, and other people in the Republic of Croatia. They also asked us for information on the number of refugee and displaced persons centres, their addresses, the numbers of people in them, and everything else they needed to know for their statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I don't intend to ask any particular question, but Your Honours may wish to focus on page 12 and you can see question, for instance, number 5 or number 11 or number 12 may be of some interest to Their Honours. And if you wish to ask any questions regarding this, fine; otherwise, I'll move on to the next document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You certainly may.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Karnavas and Your Honours. If I may comment a little. You mentioned question 12: [In English] "Do the international humanitarian organizations, in your opinion, help more Muslim or Croatian refugees or they help them both equally." Both equally. [Interpretation] 69 per cent, 69 per cent, said "both equally." This shows our citizens responded to refugees and displaced persons. So just as the office did not draw distinctions between refugees and displaced persons but provided the same assistance to both groups, the public did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. If we go on to the next document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. To know what this means it would be important to know who were the persons questioned? It's the answers of what kind of a sample? It's probably somewhere in the document, but the witness probably knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Top of page 5, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the methodology is there. The document had its methodology. This agency was active at the time in conducting various opinion polls on political issues, social issues, national issues. It was very active agency. It was by no means a pro-government agency. It was non-governmental, and they adhered strictly to the principles they held. They say 335 cases of refusal and so on and so forth. One must simply read these pages because it is in these pages that everything is explained --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, Dr. Rebic. Thank you for pointing that out to us. I don't mean to cut you off or be rude, but we need to move on so I hope you will accept my apologies. If we could look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I do accept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 1D 02627. It's in binder 1 for the Judges. 1D 02627. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And here we see that this is from the Government of the Republic of Croatia and it's a list and registration of expelled persons and returnees -- refugees, I'm sorry, in the Republic of Croatia in 1994. And if we flip -- if we go to page 2 we see at the bottom of the foreword section your name. Could you briefly tell us who prepared this report?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees of the Republic of Croatia compiled this report. It is the third census which took place in 1994, the third registration. The first, as I said, took place in 1992 in May and June when all displaced persons in the Republic of Croatia were listed. In 1993, in May, June, and July, there was a second census when we listed all the refugees from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This now is the third census in 1994 when we took a census of all of them together, both displaced persons and refugees. It was done on a very detailed sample about. About 100 pieces of information were taken from each and every person, some more important some less, including their economic situation, whether they had had a house in Bosnia-Herzegovina that they left, was their house burnt down, and so on and so forth. There is a list of all the persons who worked on this census. The agency that did it is called VIP. It was owned by Jakov Binenfeld, a wealthy citizen of Zagreb of Jewish origin, who at that time had the best developed information technology service in Zagreb. It was recommended to us that government IT establishment processed this information, but together with the UNHCR, which co-financed the project, I decided to accept Jakov Binenfeld's offer because he was the only one in Zagreb and Croatia at the time who had the best-developed and the most reliable information technology agency. The report is elaborated in great detail. You will see in it how many displaced persons and refugees there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Judges may have some questions, but before they pose any if I could focus your attention on page 20 at the bottom of the page on page 20, the English version. And in Croatian, because it may assist you, because there is some -- in Croatia it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could get Madam Usher to assist us very quickly to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if you could look at page 20 in English and I'll give you the Croatian version. And I'm most interested in focusing your --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not so much interested in the numbers where we see refugees in 1993, 269.000; and then in 1994, 183, I'm not interested in that. I'm interested in the paragraph that follows, and of course there's some handwritten notes. But perhaps can you tell us what exactly does this report say in this section? And we only have about three minutes so you need to limit your answer to three minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this report deals with the numbers of displaced persons and refugees and it compares various years. In 1992 there were 247.000 displaced persons, in 1994 there were 196.000; so there were fewer which means that between those two years many displaced persons were able to return to the liberated areas and there is a list of all the places where they were able to return, Osijek and other places. As regards refugees in 1993 there were 269.000 refugees, and in 1994 there were 183.000. And the difference is again explained here. The difference is due to the fact that some refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina, both Bosniaks and Muslims. They returned to the liberated areas, the safe areas, which were no longer threatened by war, such as Zenica, Tuzla, and Sarajevo. One should also mention that at the time, in the last few months of 1994, 150 refugees were sent back from Sweden, and they were Bosniaks, Muslims, because they had Croat passports. Sweden sent them back to Croatia because they had Croat passports, but they were Muslims. And of course we sent them back also because they were able to go back to safe areas. If the areas in question were unsafe, we did not send them back. I added a note here saying that 40 to 50 persons per week were being sent back from Sweden. We had agreed on this with the Swedish government, that they should not all be sent back at once, but that they should be sent back at a rate of some 40 persons per week to make it easier for us to accommodate them in Croatia or to send them on to Bosnia-Herzegovina if they could be sent back safely. That's it in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very, very much, and I believe it's 7.00 so, Dr. Rebic, we will need to pick up tomorrow where we left off today.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I think you have used about two hours, so you have about another two hours tomorrow.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, have a good evening. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.
